Police began investigating Brand in 2023 after multiple women came forward with allegations of assault and abuse in a Channel 4 documentary and the Sunday Times report. Prosecutors first filed five charges against Brand in April 2025, while two additional charges were brought in December.

Since the sentencing, six more women have come forward with allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand. The new allegations against Brand span from 2005 to 2015, six years after the most recent incident covered in his rape and sexual assault trial, which had accusations from 2004 to 2009.

#3322. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3321. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#3318. Big Oil, Climate Change, and a ‘Smoking Gun’

This story is published in partnership with DeSmog, the climate investigations site.

Arnold Obguia did not leave the island. According to the forecast, it was no big deal, just another tropical storm. But a few hours later, the winds escalated rapidly, bringing waves so large they almost pulled him out to sea. Clinging to a piece of broken sea wall, Arnold survived to find his house completely destroyed. Others were not so lucky.

Typhoon Rai, known locally as Typhoon Odette, battered the Philippines in December 2021. With winds of up to 167 miles per hour, extreme rainfall, violent storm surges, extensive flooding and landslides across the central Philippine archipelago, Odette ripped rooftops from houses and devastated crops, engulfing people and property in torrents of fast-flowing floodwater. A Category 5 cyclone, Odette displaced nearly 3.2 million people, killing 400, injuring over 1,000 and causing nearly a billion U.S. dollars in damages.

Now, Arnold and other victims of the typhoon are demanding their day in court, filing a civil lawsuit against oil and gas giant Shell. Their allegations: Shell helped to make the typhoon more destructive through the company’s contribution to historic greenhouse gas emissions and its funding of climate denial — despite knowing since at least 1965 that the burning of fossil fuels was the primary cause of man-made climate change.

“The forecast had initially said it was going to be a weak storm,” says Arnold from the house he rebuilt with storm debris on the tiny island of Bilangbilangan in the heart of the Philippines’ Cebu Strait. Forty four years old, Arnold is a fisherman, born and raised on the island, who earns his living catching trevally and bigeye scad, silvery-blue-green fish that swim in large schools around the region’s coral reefs.

“But suddenly the winds were different, they were very strong,” he recalls. “When I looked outside the window it was frightening because the waves were very high.” While his wife and two young daughters had taken refuge on the mainland, Arnold and his 14-year-old son had stayed behind to guard his boat and fishing equipment — the source of the family’s livelihood. “The waves were swelling and I could see the storm surge coming,” he remembers. Calculating that he might have time to better secure his boat, he ran outside only to get caught by the 20-foot waves that nearly swept him away. Terrified, Arnold held tight to the broken sea wall until, bruised and wounded by the debris whirling in the water, he was able to rejoin his son. “Thinking about my family and how much I wanted to see them again gave me the strength to hold on,” he says. Arnold and his son rode out the rest of the storm sheltering in the house of a neighbor. Hours later, when it was over, Arnold discovered his boat was broken but his family was safe. Like everyone else on Bilangbilangan, they had lost almost all their possessions. “Everyone went back to zero,” he explains. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Arnold joined the lawsuit in early 2024 when a coalition of NGOs working with communities ravaged by the typhoon organized a civil claim on behalf of the survivors. In 2025, British law firm Hausfeld agreed to take up the case in the U.K. — where Shell is headquartered —submitting full details of the claim against the oil company in July of this year.

Representing more than 100 of the typhoon’s victims, Hausfeld describes the suit as a “landmark case” that could have “major repercussions for the fossil fuel industry,” potentially paving the way for other hard-hit communities around the world to sue oil Big Oil on its home turf. The firm argues its clients suffered severe losses including serious property damage, personal injury, bereavement, psychological trauma, and loss of earnings. An announcement of the date for the first hearing to be held at London’s High Court is expected sometime early next year, says Greg Lascelles, the Hausfeld partner leading the legal team. Related Content How DC’s Progressive ‘Absolute’ Line Has Reinvigorated Modern Comics Vince Staples: ‘Hip-Hop Doesn’t Really Have Any Rules’ Alex Warren and Megan Moroney Want to Share It All You Know Rosalind Eleazar From ‘Slow Horses.’ She’ll Blow You Away in ‘Misty Green’

Shell has dismissed the lawsuit as “baseless,” asserting the company had no “unique knowledge about climate change” in an official statement.

However, evidence uncovered by Rolling Stone in collaboration with nonprofit climate news service DeSmog reveals explosive new details of Shell’s decades of climate research that warned the company burning fossil fuels could lead to worsening storms — including studies conducted at the Climatic Research Unit (CRU), the U.K.’s first specialist climate research center Shell helped to found on the campus of a university in eastern England in 1972.

Some of these documents might have been lost forever, had a sharp-eyed faculty member not rescued them from a dumpster where they’d been thrown out after the retirement of the CRU’s first director, the U.K.’s leading climatologist, Hubert Lamb. Now,preserved inside the temperature-controlled archives at the University of East Anglia a few miles outside the medieval city of Norwich, these and other files contain handwritten notes, official correspondence, and reports that hold secrets of Shell’s early climate research, detailing a program that would give the company advance warning of the numerous threats climate change posed to its business — if not to the people, like Arnold and his island neighbors, liable to suffer the most harm.

Documents from the late 1960s show Shell playing a pivotal role in establishing the center before paying the CRU to carry out an in-depth North Sea Storms Study beginning in the mid-1970s. The findings warned Shell that storms in Europe’s North Sea — home to the company’s burgeoning offshore drilling business — were increasing. Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) levels due to the burning of fossil fuels might be the most likely explanation, the Shell-funded study concluded.

These discoveries contribute to a growing body of existing evidence demonstrating that by the late 1980s the oil majors, including Exxon and Shell, knew the dangers posed by fossil fuel-induced climate change. However, a fresh look at the documents previously unearthed by other researchers shows Shell receiving further storm warnings. For example, in 1980, a Shell-sponsored study at the CRU modeling future “Scenarios for a High CO2 World,” calculated that rising CO2 levels from burning fossil fuels would “perturb the whole atmospheric circulation system,” affecting rainfall, temperatures, and winds all over the world.

By the end of the 1980s, Shell had specifically learned that global warming would likely lead to more frequent and more dangerous storms, especially in tropical regions.

Today, as the world approaches the peak of what promises to be the worst El Niño cycle in recorded history, supercharging hurricanes, heatwaves, droughts, and other extreme weather events already made worse by climate change, the documents open a rare window into Shell’s early sponsorship of climate science, illustrating how much the company knew about the risks posed by burning its products before supporting million dollar PR and lobbying campaigns that denied or cast doubt on this climate science in public.

Shell did not respond to a request for comment about the company’s historical climate research.

Geoffrey Supran, an associate professor in the department of environment science and policy at the University of Miami who is not involved in the lawsuit but who has reviewed the new documents for Rolling Stone and DeSmog, calls them “a smoking gun,” containing important evidence of “how the early climate denial machine began to be built — and when.”

“Seen across seven decades, Shell’s research looks less like scientific philanthropy and more like a public affairs strategy of ‘Know Thy Enemy,’” says Supran, “allowing the company to understand climate change early, help shape and stay close to the science, anticipate the physical, and economic threats it poses, and stay ahead of policies that might threaten business-as-usual.”

Sitting at his desk in London’s ‘Shell Tower,’ a 26-story modernist skyscraper with majestic views overlooking the River Thames and Houses of Parliament, R. O. Chalkley had a problem.

It was September 1966. The Beatles’ Revolver had reached Number One in the album charts but Chalkley was wrestling with something far more changeable: the weather.

As the director of a company-wide planning study, it was Chalkley’s job to help Shell find the most effective way of coping with variations in the demand for oil brought about by an apparently changing climate. Recent European winters had sent temperatures plunging but if Shell invested heavily in storing up larger quantities of oil to heat Europe’s homes only for the weather to turn warmer, it could prove an expensive mistake.

Luckily for Chalkley, an August 1966 article in The Times by the U.K.’s leading climatologist, Hubert Lamb, offered a possible solution. “Is our climate changing?” Lamb asked, arguing that improved understanding of the Earth’s climate history was essential for future economic planning. Hoping that the climatologist’s work might benefit Shell, Chalkley wrote to Lamb inviting him to discuss “the climatic aspects” of the company’s problem in person.

Their meeting was an instant success, launching the idea for a Shell-funded “Centre on Climatic Studies” — Lamb would search for a university to host his research, while Chalkley pitched the idea to his bosses inside Shell.

Slowly, the proposal moved up the ranks at Shell Tower and, on Oct. 1, 1969, Chalkley arranged a meeting between Lamb and a handful of high-level Shell executives.

Present at the meeting was Monroe Spaght, a former country boy from Eureka, California, now president and chairman of Shell Oil (the company’s U.S. subsidiary) and the first American managing director of Shell’s parent company, Royal Dutch. Joining Spaght was Lord Victor Rothschild, director of Shell Research, scion of the famous banking dynasty, scientist, and Second World War spy chief. Both held key positions on Shell’s Grants Committee and were “visibly enthusiastic” about Lamb’s proposal for the U.K.’s first specialist climatic research center to be housed at the University of East Anglia under the aegis of Professor Keith Clayton, dean of its brand new School of Environmental Sciences.

No record of Lamb’s 1969 pitch to Shell has yet been found but a proposal for the center written around the same time reveals that, in addition to providing enhanced weather forecasting, investigating the climate impact of burning fossil fuels was one of the center’s founding ambitions, Rolling Stone and DeSmog can reveal.

“Climatic history is particularly important because man is now disturbing the atmosphere so much (e.g. by increasing the CO2 level by burning fossil fuel) that it is difficult to disentangle long term trends from the effects of man,” stated the proposal, before promising that the center offered “a hope of long term climatic forecasting,” and would “evaluate the problems posed by such man-made changes as the CO2 level of the atmosphere.”

This message that burning fossil fuels could be altering the Earth’s climate would not have come as a surprise to either of Shell’s top men.

Spaght represented Shell Oil on the board of the American Petroleum Institute (API), the U.S. oil industry’s primary lobby group. In November 1965, API President Frank Ikard had briefed the group’s membership on the latest science linking CO2 emissions from “coal, oil, and natural gas” with future temperature increases and “changes in climate.”

Meanwhile in London, former intelligence officer Rothschild had already coordinated secret climatic research inside Shell, having commissioned the visionary British scientist James Lovelock to investigate the atmospheric consequences of burning fossil fuels. Were fossil fuels altering the Earth’s climate or could other factors be blamed? In the summer of 1965, Rothschild had dispatched Lovelock to find out.

Submitting a report in June 1966, Lovelock had confirmed that pollution from burning fossil fuels “may be responsible for large scale phenomena affecting the whole of the Earth’s atmosphere.”Although there were uncertainties over the precise impacts of different pollutants, Lovelock told Shell it was important to recognize “the almost certain fact that the climate is worsening and the probability that the combustion of fuel is responsible.

As several historians have recently documented, Shell buried Lovelock’s findings for years, and Rothschild expressly forbade him from talking to “non-Shell people” about his work.

By the late fall of 1969, however, Shell seems to have taken Lovelock’s warning seriously enough to sponsor a new climate project.

After his meeting with Spaght and Rothschild, Lamb wrote to the University of East Anglia’s Professor Clayton informing him that Shell wanted to set up a climatic research center “for their own ends.” Not only did the company want monthly and seasonal forecasts but also advice on “the more general climatic prospect over 5 to 25 years.”

Shell’s Spaght was particularly encouraging, stating that the new project would contribute to “the increase of knowledge” in general and might also be “beneficial to Shell’s operations.”

At the end of October 1969, Shell approved an initial grant of £10,000, a contribution it eventually doubled to £20,000 ($370,000 today) — a game-changing amount that, in Clayton’s words, made the Centre “a real possibility.” By 1971, BP had also put forward £3,000 and two U.K. electricity groups, £5,000. With these sums in the bag, the university agreed to provide the rest of the funding. And, in 1972, the “Climatic Research Unit” (CRU) opened its doors with Lamb appointed its first director.

From the outset, the CRU provided its sponsors with general weather forecast bulletins and a newsletter “to keep a finger on the pulse of world climate.” But, before long Shell would find an even more specific use for the CRU’s expertise.

Obtaining information about storms was about to become one of the company’s top priorities.

“The Texas of Europe” was how the British press described the massive oil fields discovered by Shell and Esso [Exxon’s U.K. subsidiary] at the start of the 1970s in Europe’s North Sea — a region notorious for its fearsome waves and gale force winds.

Naming the oil fields after local seabirds, Shell operated the enormous “Brent” field and in 1975 paid the CRU another £15,921(worth $166,000 today) to conduct a “North Sea Storms Study” that would help the company future-proof its new facilities.

It was exactly the kind of project Lamb had been waiting for, allowing the CRU to gather records dating back to the time of the Spanish Armada of 1588 — a “wealth of information” meticulously recorded by scientists, sailors, merchant traders, and amateur observers across 400 years.

The documents reveal Shell working closely with Lamb on a plan designed to identify specific dangers and improve storm prediction techniques. According to Lamb, the research would alert Shell to “forewarning signals” indicative of extreme weather events by mapping and analyzing “the severest North Sea storms of the past.” The study would also look at “variations of sea level in the North Sea region” produced by storms as well as “disastrous sea floods” and “the height of sea defences.”

With its profitable North Sea operations playing an increasingly important role in its business, Shell requested regular updates. In November 1981, Lamb sent Shell an “Interim Report,” noting that he was also keeping a watch on “current weather developments” including recent storms that had seriously damaged several North Sea oil rigs.

Citing these powerful storms, Lamb sent a further update to Shell in 1982 containing a significant new observation. According to the data, Lamb told Shell in handwritten notes, there was “some indication of an increasing storminess” since the 1950s. In November 1981, winds reaching 120 to 130 knots — equivalent to a Category 4 hurricane — had ripped two oil rigs housing over 200 people from their moorings.

This warning would come almost 10 years before the study was published, giving Shell advance notice of nearly a decade that storms in the North Sea were increasing.

Despite Shell’s appreciation for Lamb’s “useful” work, the company did not approve further funding for the storms study. Undeterred, Lamb, who had retired as the CRU’s director, completed the study in 1991, sending a copy to the head of Shell Exploration and thanking the company “for the grant which started the project.” In line with his earlier findings, Lamb wrote that his subsequent research had confirmed his observations of increasing storminess in the North Sea over the latter half of the 20th Century and he concluded that rising atmospheric CO2 levels could be considered a likely explanation.

In the cautious, circumspect style that is typical of his writings, Lamb stated: “It is not easy to point to a firmly established reason for the increase in storminess affecting northern and northwestern Europe, and the off-lying seas, since 1950. Some would probably attribute it with little more ado to the greenhouse effect expected from the increase of carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere caused by human activities.”

Over the 1980s, Shell continued to use the CRU as the company’s go-to lab for inside climate information and advance updates.

While Lamb was focusing on historic storms, in 1980 Shell funded another CRU study, “Scenarios for a High CO2 World,” investigating what a future, warmer world might look like. Using 20th Century temperature records, the CRU researchers modelled four potential future climate impact scenarios.

Specifically, the company wanted to know how changes to temperature, rainfall, and sea-levels might affect Europe’s energy consumption and agriculture — key areas of interest for Shell’s business operations.

The research was published in 1983 and extended to North America in a 1984 report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), tracked down by Rolling Stone and DeSmog. Basing their North American calculations on the methodology they had developed for Shell, the CRU researchers also submitted this second report to the oil company.

In both cases the message was the same. Increasing atmospheric CO2 produced by the burning of fossil fuels would trap ever-increasing amounts of heat within the earth-atmosphere system. Beyond increases in temperature, however, the CRU’s researchers emphasized that the overall impact would be “much more fundamental,” that it would “perturb the whole atmospheric circulation system,” affecting rainfall and winds, “indeed all of the meteorological variables,” around the world.

An even more urgent warning was delivered to Shell two years later in November 1985 when a member of the company’s internal “Greenhouse effect working group,” M. H. Griffiths, visited the CRU for a status update on the latest developments in climate science from its new director, Thomas Wigley. Although Wigley briefed Shell’s representative on remaining scientific “uncertainties” relating to the precise impacts of the greenhouse effect, he was “prepared to stick his neck out” on some key points, wrote Griffiths in a confidential 1985 internal Shell memo. This memo, detailing Griffiths visit to the CRU, formed part of a 90-page “confidential” internal company report on “The Greenhouse Effect” compiled in 1986 for Shell International, discovered by Dutch journalist Jelmer Mommers in 2018.

As Griffiths reported to Shell, Wigley warned him that although “CO2 build-up” had caused a global temperature increase of 0.5 degrees over the last 100 years, “a further 1-2 degree warming over the next 40 years” was expected — a rise “greater than any change in the last 1000 years.” And, while global warming had already caused average sea levels to rise by “some 15cm over the last 100 years,” Griffiths noted that they could rise a further 20-120cm by 2050.

Higher global temperatures would result in higher rates of evaporation, Griffiths informed Shell, meaning “Monsoon rainfall ought to increase also as should the frequency of tropical storms.”

As the scientific consensus on climate change strengthened over the course of the 1980s, the company joined forces with other oil majors under the banner of the International Petroleum Industry Environmental Conservation Association (IPIECA), a global oil and gas group that had been established in 1973 to monitor and influence environmental protection measures that might “affect the oil industry.” In 1988, IPIECA formed a Working Group on Global Climate Change tasked with producing an internal report that would brief IPIECA’s members on the newest developments in climate science. Two Shell representatives were among theWorking Group as were representatives from Exxon, Mobil, Texaco, BP, ELF, and Saudi Aramco.

“Major populated coastal areas of the globe are at risk from rising sea level, especially in undeveloped countries,” declared the IPIECA report, discovered by Nathaniel Rich, author of Losing Earth: The Decade We Could Have Stopped Climate Change in 2019. A section of the report authored by Exxon’s Senior Scientist, Brian Flannery, also warned “that the frequency and magnitude of large storms may be higher in a warmer world.” The coupling of sea level rise, and the possibility of enhanced storm surges presented “a serious risk, especially to low-lying coastal areas,” explained Exxon’s scientist.

Fast forward approximately three decades when this “serious risk” warning given to Shell was realized in the devastation wrought by Typhoon Odette. Photographs of the aftermath show buildings broken into matchsticks, crops destroyed, livestock animals killed, as well as damage to bridges, roads, ports, airports, and communication lines. In low-lying coastal areas, the strong winds, storm surges, and floods killed people instantly. More than 400 lost their lives with drowning being the most common cause of death.

On Bilangbilangan, Arnold knows he is lucky to be alive but the trauma of the typhoon stays with his whole family. They are all afraid of another storm. “After the storm, everything was washed out, the houses, the boats and everything,” he says, describing how he lost his fishing rod and other equipment. “For the community, everyone had a difficult life after the storm. Everything was devastated.”

“Honestly we are still not fully recovered,” Arnold explains. “All of our appliances, our personal belongings — very few were saved.”

By contrast, in 1989, Shell announced it was redesigning its $3-billion dollar North Sea “Troll” gas platform, raising it by 4 to 6 feet to better protect its operations against damage from the rising sea levels and more powerful storm surges predicted as a result of climate change. Reported by the New York Times as the first major project to anticipate the impacts of the greenhouse effect, a Shell spokesman told the Times he hoped that gas production from Troll would continue “for up to 70 years.”

But, just as Shell was taking these steps to protect its own operations, the company simultaneously began pouring money into public relations and lobbying campaigns denying the science of human-caused climate change.

1988 had been a trigger year for oil companies. In June, NASA scientist James Hansen had told a U.S. Senate Committee that global warming was already changing the Earth’s climate. In August, Republican presidential candidate George H. W. Bush had given a campaign speech promising to tackle the greenhouse effect with “the White House effect.” And, in November, the United Nations had formed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change to help governments develop policies aimed at preventing climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The threat to oil companies was clear. In response, they went after the science.

“No convincing evidence exists to support claims that hurricanes, tornadoes, and other extreme temperature and precipitation events are on the rise,” declared a 1995 press release from the oil-industry funded group, the Global Climate Coalition (GCC). A fossil-fuelled engine of disinformation, the GCC spread climate denial during the 1990s. Shell was one of its founding members, joining in 1989 — the very same year the company began climate-proofing its North Sea oil facilities.

Working through the GCC for the best part of a decade, Shell and the other oil majors bankrolled the group’s well-documented multimillion-dollar public relations and lobbying campaigns designed to persuade Americans that the science of climate change was uncertain and to block national and international measures aimed at tackling global warming — including the introduction of carbon taxes and U.S. ratification of the Kyoto Climate Treaty.

“Oil companies had been at the forefront of climate research right up to the moment when the world actually began to wake up to the crisis,” says the University of Miami’s Geoffrey Supran. “At which point they spent the next 30 years pretending that this was all new, uncertain, unreliable science on the basis of which no policy decisions could ever be made.”

Backed by Shell, a 1995 GCC campaign targeted concerns that global warming was increasing the risk of hurricanes, casting doubt on studies linking rising sea surface temperatures with more intense tropical storms. The campaign’s central reference was a GCC-funded report conducted by commercial weather-forecasting firm Accu-Weather that attributed public fears over increased storminess to “global warming alarmists.”

Like many of the GCC’s publications, the Accu-Weather report championed the work of a new wave of so-called climate skeptics frequently sponsored by Shell and other oil interests. While the first wave of industry-sponsored scientists, like Lamb and Wigley, were drawn from the scientific center ground, this new wave of scientists consisted of a small number of outliers, occupying fringe positions from which they waged a relentless contrarian war, variously arguing that computer-based climate modeling was unreliable, that temperature predictions were inaccurate, or that high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide would improve plant growth.

Amplified by the GCC, this small cadre of skeptics appeared regularly in print as well as on television and radio, successfully marginalizing legitimate scientists and draining public support for climate action.

Releasing the report on the eve of a United Nations climate negotiation session in New York for maximum impact, the GCC hosted a press conference at the UN Plaza Hotel intended to “provide reporters with an overview and background of the issues under consideration at the session.” Key press releases sent out by the lobby group, however, failed to mention that the Accu-Weather report had been paid for by the GCC and its fossil fuel industry sponsors.

Shell quit the GCC in 1998 as public calls for action to address climate change intensified. But the damage was done. Proposals for a tax on fossil fuels in the U.S. had been defeated, helped by a $1.8 million campaign by the GCC. And in 2001 the Kyoto Protocol on emissions reductions was rejected by U.S. President George W. Bush — according to an internal State Department brief this decision was due in part to input from the GCC.

Early access to climate scientists like Lamb and Wigley not only gave Shell and other oil companies advance information useful for protecting their own facilities, it also provided another major advantage: a working knowledge of the uncertainties, common to any field of scientific enquiry. In the 1990s, amid international calls for curbs on greenhouse gas emissions, the industry weaponized these uncertainties to sow confusion and stall policy.

For 60 years, “the oil industry has been playing four-dimensional chess with the public affairs of climate change,” says Supran, pointing to what he calls a “four-step” playbook. “First they learn about the dangers of their products, then they scheme, then they deny, and then they delay in any way possible.”

Despite quitting the GCC, Shell remains a member of the American Petroleum Institute (API) and other industry lobby groups also accused of carrying out climate disinformation activities on behalf of the oil and gas industry. Along with Shell and other oil majors, the API is facing state-level legal action in the U.S. for its alleged role in promoting climate denial.

Today, climate denial based on the false arguments and red herrings popularized by the GCC, still persists as a powerful force in the U.S. and around the world, underpinning President Donald Trump’s withdrawal of the U.S. from the 2015 Paris Agreement as well as the administration’s rollback of domestic climate policies and unprecedented attacks on climate science.

“By obstructing climate action, those campaigns exposed all of us — particularly the vulnerable and unborn — to dangers the industry itself had long foreseen,” says Supran.

“Science has been sounding the alarm on the scale of climate harm for a long time,” says Joie Chowdhury, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). “Now, with the different climate litigation cases across different countries, the law is catching up.”

Using the same legal strategy that won record payouts from Big Tobacco in the 1990s and 2000s, the Typhoon Odette survivors’ case against Shell is the latest in a rising number of “climate deception” lawsuits being brought against oil and gas companies for actively promoting disinformation about their products through organizations like the GCC. There are currently more than two dozen such cases pending in the U.S. alone with another filed against BP in New Zealand, according to the Climate Litigation Database compiled by Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. Essentially these are fraud cases, explains Chowdhury. “We’ve seen numerous lawsuits alleging that major oil companies knew about the risks for decades, that they misled the public and helped to delay climate action while continuing to profit from fossil fuels,” she says, describing the U.S. as “an epicenter” of this type of litigation.

While the U.S. legal system is particularly well suited to class action lawsuits, opportunities for climate litigation on behalf of multiple claimants, like the Odette case, are rapidly growing elsewhere. While deception is not always at the heart of these cases, says Chowdhury, the idea that polluters should pay for the destruction their products cause is gaining traction. To date, hundreds of greenwashing and other climate accountability claims have also been filed against fossil fuel companies around the world.

Since Shell is headquartered in the U.K., the Odette claimants are suing the company in London, kickstarted by a 2022 finding of the Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines, which ruled that major fossil fuel companies can be held accountable for human rights violations caused by climate change and that affected Filipino citizens may pursue civil and legal remedies through other national courts.

It is not publicly known who is funding the Odette case. In the past, similar legal costs have often been met by philanthropic foundations or charities but the U.K. has also seen an uptick in litigation funding by private investors who see future payouts from such legal battles as a potential business opportunity.

Big Oil, however, is pushing back. Firstly through the age-old legal tactic favored by big corporations: extensive procedural fights about where cases should be heard. On October 5, the U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments relating to a petition from ExxonMobil and the Canadian energy giant, Suncor, both facing a climate deception lawsuit in Colorado, that fossil fuel companies should not be sued in state courts over their role in global warming. A ruling is expected in 2027. Raising the stakes even higher, the American Petroleum Institute and the industry’s Republican allies have also been lobbying U.S. lawmakers to give fossil fuel companies total legal immunity from climate deception cases.

“For years, fossil fuel companies have argued that climate claims belong in federal court or are matters for Congress rather than state courts,” Chowdhury says. But the “explosion in climate accountability cases” outside the U.S. including the Odette case, reduces the risk that this accountability depends on the outcome of cases in the U.S., or any one specific country, she says.

“Climate harm does not exist beyond the reach of law,” argues Chowdhury.

According to figures from the International Chamber of Commerce, climate-related extreme weather events are estimated to have cost the global economy $2 trillion over the last decade — costs that could spiral to $3.1 trillion a year by 2050.

Issuing an official response to climate lawsuits, Shell maintains that “litigation aimed at individual companies is not an effective way to reduce global emissions.”

Roosters crow and dogs bark as Arnold speaks on a video call via a translator patched in from Manila. It’s late afternoon on Bilangbilangan, a time when Arnold would usually be preparing to go fishing but today the seas are too rough. “It’s too unpredictable,” he says, looking through his window out to sea.

Every day stuck on the island is a day without income and times are tough. Before Odette, the fish catch was abundant and Arnold was easily able to provide for his family, earning up to 5,000 pesos ($80) on a good day. But Odette damaged the coral reefs that support the local fish stocks and for a period after the typhoon he went for months without income. Although things have improved since then, the catch remains smaller. On a bad day he may only catch around 400 pesos’ worth of fish, equivalent to around $6. “I’ll go out tomorrow,” Arnold says, “if the weather improves.”

As we talk, Typhoon Francisco is sweeping north with winds reaching 145 miles per hour. Satellite trackers show Francisco veering away from the Philippines but the effects of its wider storm system are being felt across the region.

Since then, 2026’s “Godzilla” El Niño has been building in the Pacific with sea temperatures predicted to reach a peak of 39.2°F above the seasonal average at the end of this year, raising the risk of supercharged Pacific typhoons. Already wreaking havoc around the world, this El Niño is expected to be the most destructive and deadly since records began, with climate scientists forecasting “a string of weather catastrophes” around the world — from intense heatwaves, wildfires and drought in some places, to torrential rain and flooding in others. In the U.S., California’s sea levels are rising threatening coastal communities with dangerous storm surges while an unprecedented series of powerful hurricanes has been hitting Hawaii since August.

Not only is climate change causing more destructive storms, recent studies show it is also likely making storms harder to predict. A study published in December 2025 concluded that Odette’s rapid intensification from a Category 1 to a Category 5 typhoon probably occurred after the storm passed over ocean hotspots — warmer patches of seawater that are occurring more frequently as a result of climate change-induced marine heatwaves. A similar phenomenon occurred in the Gulf of Mexico in 2022 when Hurricane Ian caused destruction across Cuba, Florida and the Carolinas.

“We only knew the storm was different when it was already happening,” says Arnold. “We didn’t have the foresight that it was going to be different.” Trending Stories Sade Are Not Attending Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage Judge Sets Steven Tyler Sex Assault Trial Date

Turning to the lawsuit, Arnold says he joined the case in the hope that it might give his children the chance of a better life. “Whether we win or lose, what’s important for me and the other claimants is that our message is being sent across the world to the U.K., to Shell Headquarters. We hope this case might encourage Shell to reduce their impact on the environment because at the end of the day it’s people like us who have to face the really tall waves, the really strong typhoons.”

“If we win this case,” he adds, “it isn’t just for us, the Typhoon survivors, it’s also for the generations to come.”

#3317. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3316. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

What was wrong with the headline "Engineering Jobs That AI Can't Replace"?

Different headlines appear in different places for stories. Not seeing it on the article doesn't mean that the headline appeared differently somewhere else.

#3315. New Apple TV comedy starring Elizabeth Banks, Ted Danson coming soon

Apple TV has announced a new comedy, She’s Fine, that’s coming soon with stars Elizabeth Banks and Ted Danson. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, Apple announced a high-profile new comedy in the works starring Elizabeth Banks, with later cast additions including Ted Danson and guest star Tom Selleck.

Now today that series, titled ‘She’s Fine,’ has gotten a release date and the first images have debuted.

She’s Fine premieres Wednesday, January 27 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases through March 24.

Fresh off a messy divorce, Heidi (Banks) sets out to secure a lively second act for herself and her kids. But when she stumbles into coordinating her father’s retirement community sexcapades, Heidi is forced into an unlikely alliance with his girlfriend’s perpetually single son.

Katey Sagal and Rob Delaney also star in the half-hour comedy, which hails from creators Liz Heldens and Matt Ward.

Other notable Apple TV comedies include the Owen Wilson-starring Stick, which just returned for season 2. And Bad Monkey from the co-creator of Ted Lasso and Shrinking is coming back soon too.

Are you interested in watching She’s Fine? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3313. Raye, Rosalía, and Ella Langley Lead 2027 Grammy Nominees

Raye, Rosalía, and Ella Langley led the nominees for the 69th annual Grammy Awards, which were announced Monday morning, Nov. 16.

Raye led all nominees with a staggering 11, which ties Beyoncé’s 2025 for the most nominations in a single year for a woman artist. She’s up for all three major prizes: Album for the year for This Music May Contain Hope, and Record and Song of the Year for “Where Is My Husband!” Raye also earned a nomination for Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical.

Rosalía — fresh off her historic victories at the Latin Grammys — followed close behind Raye with nine nominations, with Lux up for Album of the Year, and “Berghain” with Björk and Yves Tumor nominated for Record and Song of the Year. And Langley notched seven nominations, including Record and Song of the Year looks for her smash, “Choosin’ Texas”; Album of the Year for Dandelion; and Best New Artist.

Langley was one of four artists to score seven nominations, alongside Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Rodrigo, and Lambert (who co-wrote “Choosin’ Texas”). Other top nominees included Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas, Olivia Dean, Taylor Swift, and Geese.

For Record of the Year, “Where Is My Husband!”, “Berghain,” and “Choosin’ Texas” will compete against Dean’s “Man I Need,” Mars’ “I Just Might,” Rodrigo’s “The Cure,” Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia,” and Tame Impala’s “Dracula” remix with Jennie.

Song of the Year will also feature “Berghain,” “Choosin’ Texas,” “The Cure,” “Man I Need,” and “Where Is My Husband!”, as well as Swift’s “I Knew It, I Knew You,” Mars’ “Risk It All,” and Ariana Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me.”

And in Album of This Music May Contain Hope, Lux, and Dandelion will compete against Bridgers’ Lost Weekend, Mars’ The Romantic, Rodrigo’s You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, and Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl.

As for the last Big Four category, Best New Artist, Langley will be joined by Slayyyter, Don Toliver, Remi Wolf, Geese, Angine de Poitrine, and the Womack Sisters.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

There’s arguably no clear frontrunner for this year’s Grammys, with many of the major category contestants — including Raye, Dean, Langley, Rosalía, and Bridgers — competing in Album, Song, and Record of the Year for the first time. Of these four, Raye and Langley are the only artists without Grammys, while Bridgers has yet to win as a solo artist. (She does have several Grammys with Boygenius, and earned Album and Record of the Year nominations with the group, too.) Rosalía picked up Best Latin Rock Album Grammys in 2020 and 2023, while Dean won Best New Artist at the most recent Grammys.

This could also be the year Rodrigo finally wins a major prize, with her latest album You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love garnering the mix of critical accolades and commercial success that usually makes a Grammy favorite. Rodrigo previously won Best New Artist in 2022, and has a couple of rock prizes to her name, but has yet to win Song, Record, or Album of the Year.

Of course, all of these musicians will ultimately have to face off against two of the most established and decorated Grammy winners of recent decades: Mars and Swift. They have 14 and 16 wins, respectively, including several in the major categories. Swift could even extend her record as the artist with the most Album of the Year wins to five if The Life of a Showgirl takes home the prize.

But Swift might be even more keen on finally winning Song of the Year in 2027. It’s still the only major Grammy she hasn’t won, and this is her ninth nomination for it; it’s a striking statistic for a one of the most celebrated songwriters of her generation, in a category celebrating achievements in songwriting. “I Knew It, I Knew You,” her much touted return-to-country, definitely feels primed to break that drought, though it will probably face its biggest challenger in Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” which is undeniably the biggest song of the year from a numbers and charts perspective.  Related Content The Grammy for Producer of the Year, Non-Classical, Will Go to the Best Storyteller The 2027 Grammys’ Best Rap Album Nominees May Not Be the Usual Suspects Busta Rhymes Wants J Dilla to Get His Flowers Ella Langley’s ‘Dandelion’ Is Front-Runner for 2027 Grammys’ Best Contemporary Country Album

Beyond the major categories, the nominations for 69th Grammy Awards feature what might be one of the best showings for new rock & roll bands in years. Brooklyn outfit Geese and Quebec duo, Angine de Poitrine both feature prominently in the Best New Artist category, and picked up several nods in the rock and alternative categories. Geese earned five nomination total, while Angine de Poitrine earned four; both acts are first-time Grammy nominees.

Slayyyter, who enjoyed a breakout year with her third album, Worst Girl in America, picked up her first Grammy nods, earning four total. And Don Toliver earned his first nominations as a solo artist, after previously scoring a look for his contributions to Kanye West’s Donda.

And then there’s all the fun, strange, and exciting stuff buried in the 100 categories that comprise the Grammys. Tinashe and Underscores both scored their first nominations, as did living legend John Cale, who picked up a look for Best Song Written for Visual Media for his work on “House” from Charli XCX’s Wuthering Heights soundtrack. (Charli, meanwhile, showed up in the Best Alternative Music Album for Music, Fashion, Film.)

Bo Burnham, a previous Grammy winner for his comedy song “All Eyes On Me,” picked up two nominations for his contributions to Bridgers’ Lost Weekend. And Dolly Parton scored three posthumous nods, including two in the Country Duo/Group Performance category, and one for Best Audio Book.

The 2027 Grammy Awards will feature five new categories as well. These include Best Asian Pop Music Performance, Best R&B Collaboration or Duo/Group Performance, Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, Best Traditional Folk Album, and Best Latin Song. Those nominees and more are below.

The 69th Grammy Awards will take place Feb. 7, 2027. See the nominees below:

#3312. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.
