#3309. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3307. Where the Hell Is Harry? And More of This Year’s Biggest Grammys Snubs and Surprises

Looking over the nominees list for the 2027 Grammy Awards as they were announced this morning, some major names might jump out as missing. And while some of those omissions have perfectly reasonable explanations — BTS chose not to participate in this year’s awards, in a move that was widely read as a response to the introduction of the new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, and Drake’s Iceman literally included a bar about his decision not to submit that album  — others have us scratching our proverbial heads. For instance: Did they seriously blank Harry Styles? For real? Here’s a list of the most outrageous snubs in the 2027 Grammy nominations, plus the most pleasant surprises we’re seeing.

Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally, the fourth studio album from Harry Styles, is the kind of record not everyone gets on first listen — it’s slightly disorienting compared to the star’s past releases, but it settles in an intriguing and rewarding way over time. Seems that the Recording Academy never quite came around to it. Styles earned zero nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards. It’s hard to believe KISSCO stepped too far outside of the bounds in which he created Harry’s House, which took home Album of the Year in 2023. Both albums are the product of an artist searching to create a tangible reflection of how they listen to and experience music in their own life. Styles reconnected with long-time collaborators Kid Harpoon and Tyler Johnson for this one. While it didn’t yield hits as big as “As It Was” or “Watermelon Sugar,” its tracklist is full of ambitious swings, like the Jersey-club-influenced lead single “Aperture” and the career standout “Season 2 Weight Loss.” Fans might say that deep cuts “Are You Listening Yet?” and “Pop” would have made better single choices than “American Girls” and “Taste Back,” which are solid but feel safer in comparison. Still, with its sharp edges of dance-rock and existentialist pop, KISSCO stands out among this year’s slate of releases. It’s perplexing to see it shut out completely. —Larisha Paul

Kahan followed up his massive breakout hit Stick Season with The Great Divide, a sprawling folk-rock odyssey that grapples with love, fame, strained relationships, and — yes — his home state of Vermont. He released the 17-track album in April, and surprised fans by dropping a deluxe edition, The Great Divide: The Last of the Bugs, hours after. With songs like the heartland anthem “American Cars” and the tender gem “Orbiter,” the record solidified his stance as one of today’s most lovable and relatable stars. Kahan took all the necessary steps here: The record debuted at Number One on theBillboard 200, he performed on SNL, appeared on the cover of Rolling Stone, and has been delivering the songs to his devoted fanbase instadiums all over the world. He reportedly submitted in several categories that included Album of the Year and Record of the Year (for the title track), yet he only pulled off a nod for Best Contemporary Folk Album. It’s disappointing, to say the least, and it only makes those “Orbiter” lyrics hit harder: “California’s so much more than some awards show.” —Angie Martoccio

Anyone who’s seen Olivia Rodrigo live knows she’s a rock star, and she counts rock legends from Weezer to Elvis Costello among her fans. But it’s still a pleasant surprise to see the Recording Academy recognize that aspect of Rodrigo’s artistry, nominating her alongside the Rolling Stones, Phoebe Bridgers, and Geese (featuring her onetime dinner companion Cameron Winter) in the Best Rock Performance category. It doesn’t hurt, of course, that the nominated track, “What’s Wrong With Me,” is a collaboration with the Cure’s Robert Smith. —Brian Hiatt

It’s been a record-breaking year for women in country music, from Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” reign to female artists populating the top five slots on Billboard’s Hot Country song chart for weeks in a row. Now they dominate the entire Best Contemporary Country Album category: Kelsea Ballerini’s Mount Pleasant, Carter Faith’s Cherry Valley, Megan Moroney’s Cloud 9, Kacey Musgraves’ Middle of Nowhere and Langley’s Dandelion are the nominees. It’s the first time in history that solo female artists have nabbed every slot in this category (formerly known as Best Country Album) — and it’s a rebuke to country radio, which still prioritizes male voices despite all of this monumental success. The most surprised this morning, probably? The program directors still trying to rationalize a playlist of all bros. —Marissa R. Moss

Gearing up for the nominations, there were rumblings that this year’s Best New Artist category might be a family affair, if siblings Audrey Hobert and Malcolm Todd both made it in. Todd submitted his R&B stunner Do That Again in several categories — including Album of the Year — but was completely shut out. And while his song “Chest Pain (I Love)” was sampled on Don Toliver’s “E85,” which earned two noms for Best Rap Song and Best Melodic Rap Performance, Todd himself is not considered a nominee. Meanwhile, his sister Hobert released her smash pop debut Who’s the Clown on Aug. 15, 2025 — days before this year’s eligibility window began — but she did plenty enough in the months that followed to qualify for a Best New Artist nomination. She earned it, with her sleeper hit “Sue Me” entering the Billboard Hot 100 over a year after its release, an opening slot for Charli XCX next year, and a feverishly devoted fanbase that was eager to see her take home the award. And as Hobert recently told us, she’s loved watching award shows her entire life, and she had a blast at the 2024 Grammys, when her pal Gracie Abrams brought her to the ceremony. “I cried the entire night,” she said. “They kept bringing me Champagne. I couldn’t see straight. I was telling people crazy things. It was the best night of my life.” We’re hoping the Grammys give both of these talented sibs a better night next time around. —A.M.

It was hard to go anywhere online this year without hearing the opening refrain from “OhYeah,” the title single from Steve Lacy’s excellent July album, which soundtracked some of the more epic moments in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Beyond just the single, tracks like “Nothing” and the Erykah Badu-assisted “Pure Colour,” made for one of the year’s most innovative records, easily deserving of a Grammy nod in one of the pop categories — or, at the very least, somewhere in the Recording Academy’s ever-expanding field. (Not even liner notes?) For 2022’s Gemini Rights, he was awarded the Grammy for Best Progressive R&B Album. Surely, this year, his new work deserved some kind of recognition. —Jeff Ihaza

How many legends do you have to make great music with in a single year to get a Producer of the Year nomination? Andrew Watt produced songs and albums by Paul McCartney, the Rolling Stones, Madonna, Michael Stipe, and Brandi Carlile, but that somehow wasn’t enough for the Recording Academy. —B.H.

Four of the five nominees for Best Rock Album are fairly predictable choices: Your Favorite Toy by Foo Fighters, The Wow! Factor by Muse, Foreign Tongues by the Rolling Stones, and Frozen Charlotte by Jack White. But for the fifth slot, the Grammys made a rather surprising left turn by selecting oddball Canadian art-rock duo Angine de Poitrine’s Vol II., as opposed to safer picks like something by the Black Crowes or the Strokes. Angine de Poitrine were also nominated for Best New Artist, Best Rock Performance, and Best Alternative Music Performance. Let’s hope it’s enough for them to get Khn and Klek, as they’re known, some performance time on the show. (For the uninitiated, Angine de Poitrine play wildly high-energy shows while wearing papier-mâché masks and polka-dot costumes.) It would be a great opportunity for this group to gain a broader following, and confuse the living shit out of millions of people. —Andy Greene

The three albums that Drake released this year are nowhere to be seen in the Grammy nominations, which is how he wants it — but he is up for Best Latin Song. Yes, you read that right. The rap superstar has received a nod for his Spanish-language feature on Karol G’s “Ahí.” It’s a little ironic, considering Drake’s longstanding differences with the Academy; the last time he won a Grammy for one of his own songs, in 2019, he gave a speech about how little the awards mean to him, and he’s chosen not to submit his own work since then. But that hasn’t stopped Drake’s collaborations from receiving nods over the years, and this time he’ll be up against acts like Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso, Rosalía, and Jorge Drexler. —Maya Georgi

Hey, hey, they’re the Monkees — and their best album just got a Grammy nomination, their first since the Sixties. What finer way to celebrate the sixtieth anniversary of these legendary sunshine-pop pioneers? It’s in the category of Best Album Liner Notes, for the Super Deluxe Edition of their 1967 psychedelic smash Pisces, Aquarius, Capricorn & Jones Ltd. The nominated writer: the great Andrew Sandoval, longtime Monkees scholar and author of acclaimed books on them and the Kinks. Pisces was one of that year’s biggest hits, with classics like “Pleasant Valley Sunday,” “She Hangs Out,” and “What Am I Doing Hangin’ Round?” (The album stayed at Number One for five weeks, until it got dethroned by Magical Mystery Tour.) It’s reason to celebrate—especially since the last time a Monkees record got a Grammy nod, it was “I’m a Believer” in 1968. —Rob Sheffield

Gracie Abrams didn’t receive any nominations this year, despite reportedly submitting her third album Daughter From Hell in almost all of the Big Four categories, amongst others. The singer-songwriter had a big year, leveling up with her third studio album, which earned her her first Number One on the Billboard 200 chart. Abrams also has a history with the Academy. Back in 2024, she earned a Best New Artist nomination, and a year later she received a nod for “Us,” her collaboration with Taylor Swift. What makes things even stranger is the fact that superproducer Edgar Barrera did earn a Songwriter of the Year nod for helping Abrams write “Broke My Heart,” which appears on Daughter From Hell. If only the Academy had a good reason for this shutout. —M.G.

When the Best Album Cover category returned last year and rightfully awarded Tyler, the Creator (as well as nominating the delightful Perfume Genius), it seemed to spell good fortune for the coming years. But this next class of nominees are … a little bewildering. A poignant photograph of Mavis Staples might be the most intriguing of this batch, and Rapsody’s God Gotta Afro & Gold Hoops makes a strong impression, too, but you’d think Charli XCX’s hotly debated Music, Fashion, Film photo shoot with male muses John Cale, Marc Jacobs, and Martin Scorsese might have been worth discussion. Same with Slayyyter’s Wor$t Girl in America, whose neon-red dollar-sign motif dominated 2026, and let the listener know exactly what to expect from her scuzzy electroclash breakthrough. How about the negative close-up of Kelela for New Avatar, a plant preserved in amber for L’Rain’s Fata Morgana, or the hand-painted illustration of Underscores’ hometown mall for U. Where were any of these stunning covers? Instead, the nominees are full of head-scratchers that leave us wanting more. —Jaeden Pinder

For all of the talk of rap’s faltering relevance in the mainstream, it’s surprising to see Baby Keem’s long-awaited album Casino, easily one of the best rap projects of the year, get mostly shut out from the awards. “Good Flirts,” the record’s standout track featuring Kendrick Lamar and a pitch perfect Momo Boyd, is up for Best Rap song, but in a Best Rap Album field that includes Ye’s, uh, controversial project Bully, it’s a shame not to see one of rap’s brightest young stars get more recognition. —J.I.

Björk may be one of the most recognizable and innovative names in music, but in her three decades as a solo artist, she has yet to be recognized in the Grammy’s Big Four Categories — until now. The Icelandic singer received nods in both the Record of the Year and Song of the Year categories for her work on Rosalía’s symphonic pop banger “Berghain.” Björk not only offers her signature vocals on the track, she also helped write it. And believe it or not, Björk has yet to win a Grammy of any kind in all those years. Could this finally the year she takes one home? —M.G.

If you follow the Yellow Brick Road deep into the Grammy nominations, you’ll find some artists heading off against one another as unusual adversaries. Wicked: For Good is up against The Wizard of Oz at Sphere in the Best Compilation Soundtrack for Visual Media category. Michelle Obama will be campaigning against Lil Jon, Michael J. Fox, Paul McCartney, Tim Curry, and Dolly Parton in the Best Audio Book field. Ariana Grande’s “immersive mix” of Petal will be facing off against Frank Zappa’s One Size Fits All in the Immersive Audio Category. And finally something’s about to happen with Mitski when she finds herself lobbying to win Best Recording Package for Nothing’s About to Happen to Me over John Lennon’s Power to the People. May the most surprising artist win! —Kory Grow

FLO and Ravyn Lenae are R&B stars, pop stars, something in-between stars — essentially, they’re everything but 2027 Grammy Award nominees. The British girl group missed out on nominations for their second studio album, Therapy at the Club, which seemed an obvious nominee for Best Progressive R&B Album. Blue Island, the third studio album from Lenae, on the other hand, could have realistically lived anywhere between the genre categories given its expansive sonic palette. In that regard, Lenae and FLO’s shutouts also speak to the limitations of how the Grammy Awards categorize music and how artists who move fluidly between genres are often relegated to an odd gray area as a result. “Leak It,” the engrossing lead single from Therapy at the Club, blows away nearly everything nominated in the Best Pop Duo/Group Performance category, and Blue Island standouts “Potential” and “Handle” wouldn’t have been out of place in Best Alternative Music Performance. Turns out Lenae was right when she sang: “Know I might be more than you could handle.” —L.P.

This year kicked off with a string of hotly anticipated rap albums, including A$AP Rocky’s Don’t Be Dumb, the culmination of almost a decade’s worth of hype. The album was a clean, cohesive take on rap from a generational icon and included some of Rocky’s most consistently entertaining material. After debuting at Number One, Rocky went on to deliver one of the year’s biggest rap tours and even dropped more songs on a deluxe version of the album, all while campaigning pretty heavily for the album’s Grammy consideration. That he received no nominations is a bit surprising, and feels a tad rude. —J.I.

This year’s country nominees include familiar faces like Lainey Wilson, Kacey Musgraves, and Chris Stapleton, but more than a few left-field surprises from outside the genre. The biggest curveball might be Black Francis of the Pixies, who scores his first-ever Grammy nomination in the Best Country Song category. The unlikely nod comes via Stephen Wilson Jr., who interpolates the Pixies’ “Where Is My Mind?” in his nominated song “Hardwired.” Queen Latifah also lands her first country nomination, thanks to her appearance on an all-star remake of Dolly Parton’s Seventies classic “Light of a Clear Blue Morning.” That collab with Parton, Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, and Reba McEntire is up for Best Country Duo/Group Performance, where it will face off with another first-time country nominee, Mumford & Sons, nominated for their song with Stapleton, “Here.” John Mayer’s in that race too for yet another collab featuring Lainey Wilson — the guitarist plays some licks on her listicle song “Phone, Keys, Wallet.” —Joseph Hudak

Contributors: Maya Georgi, Andy Greene, Kory Grow, Brian Hiatt, Joseph Hudak, Jeff Ihaza, Angie Martoccio, Marissa R. Moss, Larisha Paul, Jaeden Pinder, Rob Sheffield

#3306. Apple Notes adds a powerful new advantage in iOS 27.3

There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a new advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI.

Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a big upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week, iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many new capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

The one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole new set of powers with the new update.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. One common example is that I’ve been able to have Siri save a link to the webpage I’m currently viewing inside a note, and even specify exactly where in the note I want it to go.

In theory, third-party notes apps may be able to offer similar controls sometime next year when app skills officially launch. For now though, anyone who wants to control their notes app by voice—or via Spotlight, as I tend to do on my iPad Pro—have another reason to use Apple Notes.

Have you tried Siri AI’s new Notes features in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3305. Poetry for Engineers: Of Code and Shortleaf Pine

Read Ralph Earle’s poem from the November 2026 issue

After retiring from IBM as a senior software engineer in 2017, Ralph Earle has published two poetry collections.

I step into the warm moist airamong the columns of the pines,their net of twigs and rootscomplex as any lines of code.

The trees purify and anchor.Their branches balance my restlessness.

Their calling is to be present,mine to develop apps. Our tasksverge toward a common logic:living filaments of root, of interface.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. While at IBM, he coauthored Enterprise Computing with Objects: From Client/Server Environments to the Internet for Addison-Wesley’s Bloch-Jacobson-Rumbaugh Object Technology Series, and he published articles in technical journals, including IEEE Computer Magazine, IBM Systems Journal, Distributed Computing, Management Directions, and Object Magazine.

In retirement, Earle has flourished in a second career as a poet. His poetry collections are Everything You Love Is New (Redhawk Publications, 2024) and The Way the Rain Works (Sable Books, 2015). He has been nominated for the Pushcart Prize three times and comanages a monthly poetry series at a Chapel Hill, N.C., bookstore. His poems have appeared in many print and online outlets, including The Sun, Carolina Quarterly, and Sufi Journal.

Love of the complexity behind the interfaces.

#3304. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3303. Beyoncé Makes History as First Artist to Earn 100 Grammy Award Nominations

When Beyoncé sang “I’m one of one, I’m number one, I’m the only one/Don’t even waste your time trying to compete with me” on the Renaissance song “Alien Superstar,” she wasn’t exaggerating. Following the announcement of the 2027 Grammy Awards nominees Monday morning, the musician has reached a new history-making milestone at the Grammys. She is the first artist to earn 100 Grammy Award nominations.

Beyoncé’s 100th nomination came in the Best R&B Solo Performance category for “Morning Dew (Donk),” the archival release she surfaced in time with the 20th anniversary of her second solo studio album B’Day, though the song itself dates back to the Beyoncé era.

She set the record for most nominations in Grammy Awards history back in 2024 when she earned 11 nods for the 2025 Grammy Awards, breaking her 88-nomination tie with her husband Jay-Z and bringing her total to 99 nominations. The pair are trailed in nominations by Paul McCartney with 84, Quincy Jones with 80, and Chick Corea with 79.

At the 2023 Grammys, Beyoncé became the most awarded artist in Grammy Awards history with 32 total wins, having won Best Dance/Electronic Album, Best Traditional R&B Performance, and Best R&B Song that night. When she returned for the 2025 Grammys, having released Cowboy Carter, her country opus and the second part of a supposed three-act album trilogy, she extended her record with three more awards, including her first Album of the Year win, bringing her total to 35. It stands as the third most-nominated album with 11 nods.

This year, Raye tied the record Beyoncé set at the 2025 Grammys for most nods in a single year by a woman. Her album This Music May Contain Hope is nominated across 10 categories, plus she has earned a nomination for Songwriter of the Year. Earlier this week, Beyoncé spoke about Raye in an interview with i-D, saying, “I’m also so proud of Raye, who wrote some of the songs on The Gift. She has had such an anointing. You hear the vulnerability and wisdom in her voice.”

Two more artists she shouted out scored big acknowledgments for the 2027 Grammy Awards, too. Sienna Spiro, the bluesy UK singer who broke through this year, is up for Best New Artist. “I’ve known her family well for quite some time,” Beyoncé said. “I heard her sing when she was a kid, discovering her voice, and I can’t articulate the pride she brings me. What a God-given talent!”  Trending Stories Raye, Rosalía, and Ella Langley Lead 2027 Grammy Nominees Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on 'Fallon': 'This Does Feel Like a Happy Era' Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony St. Vincent and Metallica Honor Iron Maiden at Rock Hall (With a Jack Black Assist)

She extended her praise to Olivia Dean, who won Best New Artist at the 2026 Grammy Awards and has earned six nominations for next year’s show. “I also love and respect Olivia Dean,” she said. “These beautiful women are all kind, have grace and write and produce their own music. It gives me goosebumps. I just burst with pride when I see them.”

It will be a long while before anyone conquers the records Beyoncé has set, but she seems hopeful the future is in good hands.

#3299. Will Miranda Lambert Break the Producer of the Year Glass Ceiling?

The Grammys’ Producer of the Year category isn’t typically one that commands the same red-carpet dazzle as the artist races, but that will change this year with the nomination of Miranda Lambert. The rare female contender in a field that has only been won by men since its introduction in 1975, Lambert is up against Tony Berg (Sombr, Phoebe Bridgers), Noah Goldstein (Rosalia), Mike Sabath (Raye), and D’Mile (Bruno Mars, Victoria Monet).

Whoever takes home the trophy, it will be a first win for the nominee, though this marks D’Mile’s fourth time at bat. But a victory for Lambert, who co-produced the biggest song of 2026, Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” and its accompanying album, Dandelion, would mean recognition for the country genre, something this category hasn’t seen since T Bone Burnett‘s 2002 win on the heels of O Brother, Where Art Thou?

Even rarer: a nominee who’s a woman. Previous female candidates for this award include Linda Perry in 2019 (she tried again this year for her work with Dolly Parton and Paris Jackson), and Janet Jackson in 1990, alongside Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. What gives Lambert the edge over her fellow female production predecessors is the fact that she’s had her own career as a successful music artist for two decades, giving her a kind of credibility that the other contenders can’t claim. Lambert has the industry’s respect, and that counts for something when it comes to Grammy voting.

Breaking this glass ceiling would also be a huge win for those who have been advocating for women who work behind the scenes. The nonprofit We Are Moving the Needle (full disclosure: I serve on the soundboard) notes in its 2023 “Fix the Mix” report that only 3.2 percent of key technical credits in the Grammys production field categories were for women and non-binary people. Women have fared better in classical music, but with numbers that hardly call for applause. Trending Stories Raye, Rosalía, and Ella Langley Lead 2027 Grammy Nominees Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on 'Fallon': 'This Does Feel Like a Happy Era' Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony St. Vincent and Metallica Honor Iron Maiden at Rock Hall (With a Jack Black Assist)

It’s also worth noting that several nominated female artists, among them Rosalía and Ariana Grande, are also known to produce their own work.

Now back to the red carpet. Not to slag on the personal styles of Berg, Goldstein, et al., but Lambert will bring some much-needed shine to the role of producer. Expect rhinestones, glitter, and ass-kicking boots to go along with her Grammy noms showing, which includes a Best Country Duo/Group performance nod for Lambert’s feature on Kacey Musgraves’ “Horses and Divorces.” Fellas, take note.

#3295. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

BTS fans who haven’t kept up with new developments around the Grammy Awards over the past few months may be surprised to see the seven-piece absent from this year’s slate of nominations. Before any disappointment settles in, know that this was by the group’s own design.

Back in July, BTS announced their decision to not participate in the 2027 Grammy Awards. Their comeback album ARIRANG, released in March as their first studio album in almost six years, fell within the eligibility period for the 2027 Grammy Awards, but was not submitted for consideration.

“We decided not to participate in the Grammys this year,” BTS said in a statement translated from Korean, adding that the members “hope that music can be heard and loved by itself rather than being divided by region or language.”

The choice to sit out of the 2027 Grammys came shortly after the introduction of the new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, which recognizes “artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including but not limited to K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages,” according to the Recording Academy. This extends to singles and tracks only, not albums.

In response to BTS, Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason jr. came to the defense of the category. “I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision,” he said. “The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists.”

Just two weeks later, after speaking with stakeholders, Mason jr. said the Recording Academy would take criticisms of the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category into deeper consideration. “Regardless of our intent and desire to be even more inclusive, there are some artists in this space who feel that this category isn’t representing the music they work so hard to create, in the way they wish,” he said. “The management and Board are committed to working together to keep pace with that progress and ensure the musicians we intend to honor feel truly seen and heard by our actions.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The conversations did little to change the course of the Recording Academy’s overall decision to debut the category in 2027. “By far, the loudest feedback we heard was from people who were enthusiastic supporters of the category, fellow music creators expressing their encouragement for keeping it,” Mason jr. said in October. “We understand this conclusion will not satisfy everyone, and that never feels good. But at the same time, we are confident it’s the right conclusion for the music community overall.”

The following day, Stray Kids joined BTS in opting out of submitting their eligible releases for the show. JYP Entertainment confirmed the eight-piece group allowed the eligibility period, which concluded on Aug. 28, to pass without action. After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

#3291. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon and Best Buy, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

On Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console. Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games. During this promotion, each of the following is $39.99:

Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. Games like Donkey Kong Bananza retail for upwards of $69.99, so you're saving as much as $30 on these games during this week-long promotion. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale.

Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Use price tracking tools to determine if the deals you're keeping tabs on are actually a deal. If you feel like that's too much work, we already do that for you, so follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products makes you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3290. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3286. I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.
