#3228. Donald Trump Rages At ’60 Minutes’ Report On Lack Of U.S. Preparedness For Iran’s Drone Counterattacks

The latest 60 Minutes featured Norah O’Donnell’s report on U.S. military failures at the outset of the war with Iran, in which the Tehran regime launched drone attacks on American bases, including one that struck an Army command post in Kuwait and killed six soldiers.

On Monday, Donald Trump went after the newsmagazine, writing on Truth Social, “The new people running 60 Minutes are even worse than their predecessors.”

Trump wrote, “A recent study on an attack in the early stages of Iran was not correctly stated. Since February 28, 2026, the start of Epic Fury, Iran has fired between 8,000-9,000 One-way Attack Drones. Only 2 of them got through, resulting in U.S. fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Likewise, Iran has fired about 2,000 Ballistic Missiles. Only 1 out of the 2,0000 got through, and caused U.S. fatalities (Jordan). Translation: 99.99% of Iranian missiles and drones have been shot down or, in any event, not caused U.S. deaths. CENTCOM defensive measures have been historically effective. No one in the World has the ability to do so well. All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes ‘report.’ Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Related Stories News Willie Geist To Depart MS NOW's 'Morning Joe,' Will Expand NBC News Role And Continue To Host 'Sunday Today' Politics Bowen Yang Returns To 'Saturday Night Live' As Jensen Huang In Cold Open That Skewers Tech Billionaires' Susceptibility To Honey Pot Plots

But the 60 Minutes report, the result of an eight month investigation, included an interview with Major Stephen Ramsbottom, who filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress, calling for an investigation into why there was not adequate protection from attack drones. He said that at Port Shuaiba, an Army command post that is about 65 miles from Iran, there was “nothing there” to protect from an aerial attack. Watch on Deadline

“The site had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance,” he said.

The segment also featured other interviews, including with family members of the victims, as well as satellite imagery that showed the scale of damage that had not previously been disclosed by the Pentagon. Among the family members featured was Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among the service members killed.

CBS News has not yet commented on Trump’s post.

The show underwent a shakeup in May, replacing its executive producer with Nick Bilton and three correspondents — Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi and Scott Pelley — fired. They have made claims of CBS executive interference on stories, including ones that are critical of the Trump administration. The network has denied those claims and has said that they are part of the editorial process under editor in chief Bari Weiss.

Trump sued 60 Minutes in 2024 after it aired an interview with his rival in the presidential election, Kamala Harris. The lawsuit, over the way that Harris’ interview was edited, was widely seen by legal experts as baseless, but the network, seeking the Trump administration approval for its sale to Skydance, settled the litigation.

Cleaning windows is one of my favorite quick tasks because it takes so little time. But even after wiping the glass spotless using my go-to white vinegar and dish soap solution and dusting the windowsills, there is always one specific spot I often overlook in my regular cleaning routine.

In fact, it’s the one place that nobody bothers to look at — dusty window tracks. These usually contain all sorts of grime, from dust and debris buildup to dead bugs; they are also notoriously tricky to clean properly. Even a narrow vacuum attachment isn't enough to get deep into window tracks and reach those awkward corners.

That was until I found this clever hack that simply involves a popular pantry staple that you’ll probably have in your kitchen. What’s more, professional cleaners swear by this quick cleaning trick — that only takes minutes. Here’s why and how you use it.

Baking soda is a versatile powerhouse for tackling everyday home issues — from breaking down stubborn stains to neutralizing unpleasant odors. Beyond these common uses, though, it also proves to be effective at deep cleaning window tracks.

This is because baking soda acts as a mild abrasive that can lift grime with ease (scratch-free), and when combined with white vinegar (my go-to), it can easily create a great cleaning solution with its natural properties.

If you want to know more, check out what makes baking soda and white vinegar so good at cleaning. Just avoid these 7 things you should never clean with baking soda.

Start by clearing out any loose debris or dust, using a narrow nozzle attachment on a powerful vacuum cleaner. Next, sprinkle a layer of baking soda along the dirty window track before spraying with white vinegar.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Leave to sit for about five minutes to allow the fizzing chemical reaction to get to work on the ingrained dirt and dust. If the track is especially grimy, leave it for up to 15 minutes.

Then grab an old toothbrush or small bristle brush to gently scrub away the grime from top to bottom — not forgetting to tackle the corners and awkward crevices. You’ll see the dirt will easily lift off, making the task quick and hassle-free.

After removing dirt and debris from the tracks, wipe away any remaining baking soda and vinegar with a paper towel or microfiber cloth. Then finish the job by cracking open the window so the track can air-dry completely.

So if you want to keep your windows looking spotless all year round, be sure to include this simple 5-minute trick in your regular cleaning routine.

#3226. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

#3223. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

#3222. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3221. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

The Halliday G2 AI smart glasses are a step in the right direction, delivering camera-less specs with helpful AI features in a comfortable yet chunky (and dorky) design. But these smart glasses offer a near-identical experience to their rivals, all while not quite hitting the mark. Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When I first heard of Halliday making a splash back at CES 2025 by putting an "invisible" built-in display into its smart glasses, I was amazed by what the future of smart specs holds. Now, the company has refined its AI smart glasses in the Halliday G2, but this time, it isn't quite as revolutionary.

With its dual micro LED engines and waveguide optics on both lenses to deliver a simplistic green dot matrix style text, an open-ear audio system for personal sound and a bundle of features utilizing a Halliday AI assistant, the Halliday G2 AI smart glasses are a subtle pair of specs made for seamless daily wear. Well, I say "subtle" loosely, as everyone will know that you're wearing smart glasses with these on. And wait, many of these features sound a little too familiar...

These aren't just taking cues from the Even Realities G2, as the Halliday G2 offers like-for-like features in the exact same waveguide display format. I mean, it's even called "G2," for pete's sake! From the Meeting Flow feature that can summarize, research and transcribe conversations in meetings, which is just the Even Realities G2's Conversate feature, to the Cheat Sheet feature that acts as a teleprompter, which is just Teleprompt on the Even Realities G2, there's not a lot here to pick these over its clear inspiration.

But that's not to say its features aren't handy to use, especially when it comes to its Halliday AI, which is snappy at answering whatever you ask. Along with its informative dashboard (such as displaying the time, weather and more), notifications that are clear to read and its helpful Translate feature, there are day-to-day benefits of wearing the Halliday G2s. That said, it's still held back by other annoyances, like a subpar open-ear audio system and a Stealth Mode that doesn't do a good job at being "stealthy."

But are these the best smart glasses for you? After wearing the Halliday G2 daily, here are my thoughts.

Dual micro-LED, 600 x 300 per-eye resolution, 1,600 nits peak brightness

The Halliday G2s have clearly come a long way from their first iteration, making for a commendable pair of AI smart glasses that focus on everyday wear with helpful features, rather than "pervy glasses" with a camera in them.

When first seeing the Halliday G2, I made an all-too-quick assumption that these would give my head and ears a tough time. These are thick, blocky specs, and I could almost see how much they weigh from the look of them. But I was wrong.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Coming in at just 1.7 ounces, the Hallifay G2s are actually one of the more comfortable AI glasses I've worn. The magnesium alloy frame keeps the weight off, but the glasses themselves have a good distribution of weight with the tech that is housed in their temples.

Not quite as light or slim as the Even Realities G2 (1.2 ounces), but around a similar size and weight to the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) at around 1.79 ounces.

While I wouldn't say these feel premium to the touch, especially for the price, I would have these smart specs sitting on my face all day without being irritated by sore ears or frame imprints on my nose or around my eyes.

Most of its tech, from the 210 mAh battery to the open-ear audio it boasts, is housed in the thick temples (also like the Ray-Ban Meta specs). This makes them naturally thick, but this works out, as it makes gesture control along the right temple easier to manage. That includes tapping and swiping to navigate around in-display menus and features.

It takes a little while to get the hang of, but it works like a charm once it clicks, and the bar-like temples make it easy to swipe and slide a finger along.

You'll also find a Halliday G2 hard case, and it's sturdy, stylish and sizeable enough to easily slip in the G2s and close its strong magnetic clasp. It's no Even Realities G2 smart case that charges the glasses, but it does a fine job of keeping the Halliday G2s protected.

This is one of the first signs of similarities between the Halliday G2 and Even Realities G2. But this is a nice trait to share, because it's wonderful to have a discreet display that blends into the real world as an overlay that's easy to see and read.

Using dual micro-LED engines to cover both lenses, the Halliday G2s feature binocular waveguide displays for a minimal, yet extremely helpful, dashboard right in front of your eyes.

As with the Even Realities G2, the display is made up of green dot-matrix-style text, akin to the Pip-Boy from "Fallout." It's not obtrusive, and it makes it easy to glance at while going about your day. It helps that the waveguides have a 600 x 300 per-eye resolution and a whopping 1,600 nits of peak brightness. And yes, that means I could clearly see the display even during bright days (those are now limited in the U.K.).

Whether it's notifications coming in via your smartphone or the dashboard displaying the weather forecast for the next few hours, text is clear, bright and sharp, yet doesn't overtake your full real-world view, either. This is the kind of simplistic, futuristic display I've come to enjoy in smart glasses, so keep on this path, Halliday!

Having a personal HUD to show you the time, date, weather forecast and more at a glance is already a nice perk, but using the Halliday G2 to summarize conversations, translate languages in real time, give you instant answers just by asking it and view text via a teleprompter is what makes these glasses actually "smart."

The Halliday G2's key features include Meeting Flow, where live AI agents manage whole conversations (geared towards business meetings) by tracking, summarizing, transcribing and quickly researching what is said; Cheatsheet, a teleprompter that's (sort of) invisible to everyone but you, with customizable read speeds; and Translation, which can translate conversations in real time for over 45 different languages.

Meeting Flow is the star of the show, and it did a great job of getting all the key points said in one of my daily stand-up meetings and organizing this into different sections, such as having a To-Do List and a Quick Summary of everything that was said. I also quite liked the Thread Tracker, which helps you get back on topic before the conversation goes off the rails (which is a fun problem I generally have in meetings).

Now, there are plenty of AI agents that do this automatically in virtual meetings, like Google Gemini, Otter AI and plenty more. But the Halliday G2s give you a personal meeting assistant right in your view during meetings, which can be helpful to many.

Cheatsheet and Translate are also snappy in action, and I was impressed with the Halliday AI assistant being able to answer random questions on the fly. For example, while I was watching the cult classic "Twin Peaks," I asked where it was generally filmed, and it was quick to answer (it's in Snoqualmie Valley near Seattle).

Do any of these features sound familiar? They should, as you'll find all these Halliday G2 features on the Even Realities G2 — just named differently. For example, Conversate on the Even Realities is just Meeting Flow here, while Teleprompt is Cheat Sheet and Translate is... Translate.

While these features are like-for-like, that doesn't make Halliday's tools any less helpful, as they still do what they set out to do well.

Unless you're looking for thick, Spongebob-like glasses, the Halliday G2s aren't the most seamless smart glasses you can get, and they have far too much in common with the Even Realities G2, but with a couple more downsides, to stand out.

I can almost hear Homer Simpson shouting "Neeerd!" out of his car when I put on the Halliday G2s, and that alone makes me avoid wearing these in public.

The G2s are clearly smart glasses, as everyone I came across had pointed out at first glance. That's not such a terrible thing, but it's just how thick and bulky the smart specs are that makes them unappealing. Of course, glasses come in all shapes and sizes, and some frame styles are better suited to others. Some may enjoy the bulkiness, but there is a limit to frames being too thick, too.

Along with this, it's a shame there is only one style of the Halliday G2s, unlike the many different frames of the Ray-Ban Meta lineup and the couple of options the Even Realities G2 offers.

While the waveguide displays are discreet, others can still see the green light from the lenses at certain angles. That's why the Halliday G2 smart glasses have a Stealth Mode, so you can subtly read incoming messages or AI conversations without that green hue people may be able to see.

Or, that's what it wants to do anyway. In reality, it simply dims the green text on the waveguide displays, but it's still able to be seen at different angles (as my friends have confirmed). It's not as noticeable when Stealth Mode is turned off, but I wouldn't exactly call this stealthy.

At the very least, Stealth Mode on the Halliday G2s aren't as creepy as smart glasses with cameras, seeing as it's just text.

The only major difference between the Halliday G2 and Even Realities G2 is that the former comes with an open-ear audio system, much like the Ray-Ban Meta glasses. You can hear phone calls, listen to music or podcasts and hear a very annoying clicking sound with each action you do.

I'd prefer to not have any audio in smart glasses aimed at being everyday specs for the usual glasses wearer, especially when sound easily leaks out for everyone to hear what you're listening to, and it sounds more hollow than anything else. I also imagine the G2's battery takes a hit from this, being just around 12 hours before needing a charge. Not bad, but the Even Realities G2 can last a couple of days before needing a boost.

I understand that it's trying to be the all-in-one system for your face, so you no longer need one of the best earbuds, but it's far from accomplishing that task. And yes, I turned off that navigation click as soon as I heard it, which also meant turning off the ringtone.

The Halliday G2 are the type of AI smart glasses that I'm a fan of, offering a comfortable fit for all-day wear with helpful AI features that are intuitive to use and snappy in action. Being able to check the time or weather on the fly without having to take out your phone, summarize conversations with key talking points and translate other languages are huge perks to have sitting on your face.

But the Halliday G2s succumb to the usual problem with smart glasses: they look too "smart." That's fine if big, chunky frames suit your style, but when the Even Realities G2 does it all better at the same retail price, but in a more casual design, then it's harder to recommend these over its competition.

While the Halliday G2 AI smart glasses are a step in the right direction, there are still a few features and design choices that the best smart glasses we recommend do better.

#3218. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

"iOS 27.3 adds three new features I've used almost every day", "Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving". What's with these terrible clickbait titles lately? Did we go back to 2014?

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

Which new iOS 27.3 features have you been enjoying in the beta? Let us know in the comments.

#3217. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3216. Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac

This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3213. Baidu’s AI cloud revenue nearly doubles, but ads pull sales down again

Ads are now under half of Baidu’s core revenue. Baidu AI Cloud carried the quarter, profit returned at RMB1.4bn, and Ernie still trails DeepSeek and Moonshot, Bloomberg reported.

The Baidu Building, the company’s headquarters in Beijing

Baidu’s AI cloud infrastructure business nearly doubled in the third quarter. Its revenue rose 94% from a year earlier to RMB8.2bn. It still could not lift the group. Total revenue fell 1% to RMB30.8bn ($4.60bn) as Baidu’s search advertising kept shrinking.

The figures come from Baidu’s third-quarter results, published on Monday. Bloomberg reported that it was Baidu’s sixth straight quarterly revenue drop. The total was in line with the average analyst forecast.

Revenue from online marketing services fell 22% to RMB11.9bn. Ads now make up 48% of Baidu General Business, down from 62% a year earlier. That unit holds search, cloud and apps. It grew 1% to RMB25.0bn. Streaming service iQIYI, which Baidu reports on its own line, fell 10% to RMB6.0bn.

Baidu groups its AI products into one line, Baidu Core AI-powered Business. It brought in RMB13.2bn, up 37%, and made up 53% of General Business revenue, against 39% a year earlier. Baidu notes that these figures come from unaudited internal management accounts.

Most of the growth came from Baidu AI Cloud. Revenue from GPU Cloud, which rents out AI computing, rose 191% from a year earlier and 43% on the previous quarter. Revenue from outside customers’ token usage on Qianfan, Baidu’s model platform, rose 1,159%.

The rest of the AI line was flat or worse. AI Applications held at RMB2.6bn. AI-native marketing fell 15% to RMB2.4bn. Baidu blamed a tough economy and rising competition. It also cited its own choice to put user experience ahead of near-term revenue in AI Search.

“Our long-term investments in full-stack AI are translating into meaningful growth at scale,” said Robin Li, Baidu’s co-founder and CEO.

Net income attributable to Baidu was RMB1.4bn ($208m). A year earlier, Baidu reported a net loss of RMB11.2bn after an impairment charge on assets in its core business. Operating income was RMB626m, a 2% margin. Adjusted earnings were RMB6.78 ($1.01) per American depositary share.

Operating cash flow was RMB2.8bn. Baidu held RMB276.6bn in total cash and investments at the end of September. It has returned $373m to shareholders through buybacks since the start of 2026. Baidu expects to pay its first dividend before the end of 2026, subject to board approval.

“We will maintain a disciplined approach to capital allocation with a clear focus on investment returns as we continue to invest in AI,” said Haijian He, Baidu’s CFO.

This month Baidu unveiled ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview, the newest model in its family. Baidu says it ranks second among open-source models on the Code Arena WebDev leaderboard. The launch follows Baidu’s claim that its AI research agent sped up work on the model.

Bloomberg reported that the Ernie series has fallen out of the top tier and lags upstarts DeepSeek and Moonshot. Rivals Tencent and Alibaba have pulled ahead, it said. Alibaba launched its Qwen4-Max model on Monday morning.

Baidu’s chip unit, Kunlunxin, expects its M100 inference chip to be ready for volume production by the end of 2026. The unit is preparing a Hong Kong listing. Bloomberg News has reported that the debut could slip to next year.

Baidu “lacks the scale to compete with China’s tech platforms”, Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Robert Lea and Jasmine Lyu wrote.

Apollo Go, Baidu’s robotaxi service, reached 30 cities as of October. Its fleets drove about 34 million autonomous kilometres in the quarter. Baidu doubled its fleet in Dubai, where Apollo runs on Uber. In London, it keeps testing on open roads with Uber and Lyft.

In the second quarter, ads made up 52% of General Business revenue and the AI line 50%. Baidu holds its earnings call at 7:30am ET on Monday.

#3212. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3211. Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple

Epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the company could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed new restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the company in civil contempt.

Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

Epic, on the other hand, argues that Apple deliberately circumvented the court order by introducing new rules designed to achieve the same result as those originally prohibited.

In May, Apple appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to hear the case. Apple submitted its opening brief in September, followed by supporting briefs from the U.S. government and several legal and business groups.

Those included the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Progress, and several former federal antitrust enforcers. In a nutshell, the U.S. government argued that the original injunction did not clearly prohibit Apple’s 27% commission on external purchases, but maintained that the company was correctly held in contempt for restricting how developers could display external payment buttons.

In its opening brief, Apple argues, citing multiple legal precedents, that courts must enforce the letter of an injunction rather than its broader spirit.

According to the company, there was nothing in the original injunction explicitly prohibiting it from charging commissions on external purchases or imposing additional restrictions on payment links, so it should not be held in contempt for conduct that the court order did not clearly prohibit.

In its response filed today, Epic disputes Apple’s interpretation of the injunction, arguing that the company “attempts to avoid contempt by proposing an extreme legal standard.”

[Apple] argues that a court can find contempt only if an injunction spells out the exact practice at issue–so an injunction barring Apple’s then-existing anti-steering rules left it free to implement new ones that prevent steering just as effectively. Nothing in this Court’s precedents supports that approach, which would reduce injunctions to a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

Epic argues that “Apple devised a plan to circumvent the injunction,” claiming that “Apple chose a rate of 27% for the commission, knowing that, when combined with the developers’ payment-handling costs (more than 3%), the rate for linked-out purchases would be higher than the rate for purchases using Apple’s payment system.”

As an Apple executive admitted, every “linked-out transaction is going to be more expensive to any developer * * * than an IAP transaction at 30 percent.” Apple simultaneously commissioned a “sham” report to try to provide an economic justification for the commission; the report contained an “entirely manufactured” rationale for the 27% rate.

The company also argues that “Apple tried to cover up its scheme to circumvent the injunction” by asserting privilege over more than 57,000 documents, and points to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ finding that “its Vice President of Finance ‘outright lied under oath’ when he testified about when Apple decided to impose the new commission.”

Finally, Epic asks the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple or, if the justices decide to clarify the legal standard for contempt, to send the case back to the lower courts for reconsideration under that standard.

With Epic’s response now filed, Apple has until December 14 to submit its final brief before oral arguments take place on January 11, 2027.

#3209. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3207. Apple and OpenEvidence test whether people trust AI with health questions

Up to 200,000 people in the US can join the health AI study and share HealthKit data such as sleep and lab results. Apple says that data won’t train AI models.

Apple has launched a research study and an iPhone app to learn how people use AI for health questions. The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on Sunday. It runs in the US with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform that healthcare professionals use.

The study will look at what makes people trust health AI and how good its answers are, Apple said. It will also measure how well people understand the answers and what they do next. Apple wants the findings to shape how it and the wider industry design health AI tools.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

Participants ask the study app everyday health questions. The answers use plain language and come with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. OpenEvidence draws on sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature.

Participants can also choose to share HealthKit data, such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep or lab results. Apple wants to see whether that personal data makes the answers more relevant and easier to understand. The study will also test whether the app helps people prepare for visits with their own doctors.

The App Store lists it as the Apple Health AI Study App. Its listing adds two more uses: putting personal health data in context, and building a personalised exercise or meal plan.

Consumer health tools built on large language models can give incomplete or unclear answers, Apple said. That is why it wants research on how to present health information more clearly.

Apple said it will not use study data to train AI models. Participants decide whether to share any HealthKit data or survey answers. The app has guardrails meant to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that the participant follows up with a provider.

Apple has not integrated the app with Siri or Apple Intelligence, Steve Dent reported for Engadget. Its App Store listing says that neither the app nor the study provides medical advice, diagnosis or treatment.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert Wachter, who chairs UCSF’s Department of Medicine, in Apple’s announcement.

The study is open to up to 200,000 people aged 21 or older in the US. They need an iPhone 15 Pro or later running iOS 26 or later, the models that support Apple Intelligence.

OpenEvidence teamed up with Anthropic in September to offer free medical AI to doctors. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health in January, and Microsoft and Perplexity followed in March with Copilot Health and Perplexity Health.
