#3206. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

#3205. Tired of paying for cloud storage every month? pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal is the cure for subscription fatigue

Software used to be a one-time purchase, but over time, with the addition of cloud storage and services, everything has become a subscription. One company even tried to make your car seat heaters a subscription. Count the subscriptions you’re paying for right now: iCloud, a password manager, a couple of streaming services, a music service, maybe a VPN, and whatever other app decided this year that it needed to be $4.99 per month for something that used to be a one-time purchase.

Everything is a service now, and a lot of people are hitting the point where one more monthly charge is one too many on principle alone. Cloud storage is the one that’s hardest to cancel, because your photos and files are in it. That’s exactly why pCloud’s Lifetime plans are worth a look this Black Friday: you pay once, and your storage is yours for life!

Apple gives you 5 GB of iCloud for free, which stops being enough about a week after you buy an iPhone. The irony is that they launched with 5 GB of free storage in 2011, and it’s almost laughable that it hasn’t been increased since.

After that, it’s a subscription forever. The 2 TB iCloud+ plan costs $9.99 a month, about $120 a year, for as long as you want your photos to stay where they are. pCloud’s math is different. The 2 TB Lifetime plan is a one-time payment that costs less than four years of iCloud+ at the same size, and the day you buy it is the last day you pay anything for it.

If you’ve been paying for iCloud or Google Drive storage for all of your files for the last 9 years instead of using pCloud, go do the math on how much you’ve spent.

Apple charges a lot to move from a 256 GB MacBook Air to a 512 GB one, and you can’t change your mind later with a hard drive upgrade. Storage has gotten incredibly pricey in recent years as well. pCloud Drive is your solution without breaking the bank. It’s a native Mac app that mounts your pCloud storage as a drive in Finder, so your files appear as if they’re natively on your Mac but live in the cloud until you open them. A 256 GB laptop with a 2 TB pCloud Drive behind it stops feeling small. It runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, and everything stays in sync across all of them in real time.

With pCloud Backup, backing up the folders you choose is easy and safe from a lost laptop, fire, flood, or theft. If you run a NAS at home, pCloud supports backing it up via WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP, making it a real offsite destination for a Synology NAS, not just a simple sync folder. It would be a perfect offsite backup for small businesses, remote workers, etc.

iCloud Photos is great, but it uses storage from your iCloud storage quota, which can get expensive as Apple’s cameras get better and better and file sizes keep increasing. Every pCloud plan includes pCloud Photos, a photo gallery that organizes everything by date on a timeline, automatically tags objects and scenes, and groups shots into albums by event and person.

The pCloud mobile app backs up your camera roll automatically to free up space on your iPhone; a Memories feature resurfaces older photos, as the Photos app does; and a built-in document scanner turns receipts and paperwork into PDFs without needing a separate app. Inside the app, there is also a built-in Photo Editor with crop, rotate, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows, and eight one-click filters, so quick fixes don’t require moving it back to Apple Photos.

pCloud Docs covers documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, text, and markdown with six built-in editors and real-time collaboration, all from the browser or the mobile app. If your household is split, with one person on Microsoft, Apple, or Google, pCloud can pull in files from Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Facebook. That’s the easiest way I’ve seen to get everyone’s files into one place without needing to download and reupload everything.

Files and photos aren’t the only benefit of joining the pCloud ecosystem. pCloud Pass is a password manager that works across all devices, browsers, and operating systems, with one-click login, form filling, and a generator for strong, unique passwords. Passwords are still hard, and most people are either paying monthly for a manager or reusing the same three passwords. A lifetime license solves the annoying aspects of using a dedicated password manager app or being locked into Apple’s or Google’s systems.

pCloud Encryption is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption for your most sensitive files. In plain language: files in your Crypto folder are encrypted on your Mac before they upload, and only you hold the key. pCloud can’t read them, and neither can anyone else. It’s the right place for tax returns, scans of your birth certificate, and anything else you’d rather not have sitting in a regular sync folder.

Here’s the deal you’ll want to pay the most attention to: pCloud offers an exclusive 3in1 Bundle, because it knocks out two more subscriptions at once. It’s 3 TB of Lifetime storage plus Lifetime pCloud Pass and Lifetime pCloud Encryption, and it’s the only offer that includes everything you need to ditch a vast majority of your subscriptions. Count up what this level of storage and functionality would cost you over three or four years, and you’ll see how incredible of a deal it is. If you don’t sign up today, you’ll end up regretting it in 2030.

pCloud’s Black Friday pricing runs from November 13 through November 28. Every plan is a one-time payment with Lifetime access, no subscription, and no renewal.

You also get to choose where your data is stored, with data centers in Luxembourg and the United States, and everything is protected in transit with TLS/SSL. With pCloud, it’s your files and your rules, and one Lifetime deal protects everything.

If you’re tired of paying for storage every month, this is the week to stop. Grab pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal before it ends on November 28.

The best time to sign up for pCloud’s lifetime deal was 9 years ago. The second best is today.

#3204. Lutnick joins Trump’s China trip as Congress moves to tighten chip curbs

Bessent says new AI chip curbs are unnecessary. A New York Times investigation ties Lutnick’s family firm to a Malaysian data centre that may serve Tencent, as lawmakers ask why Commerce held back.

Howard Lutnick in the Oval Office at his swearing-in as US commerce secretary on 21 February 2025.

Congress is lining up behind bipartisan AI chip curbs aimed at China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says it is not needed. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, the official many lawmakers blame for weak enforcement, is set to fly to China with Donald Trump this week.

Bloomberg reported on Sunday that the bill, which also covers chipmaking equipment, could pass within weeks. Lutnick is expected on Air Force One for Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping at the APEC summit, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

“I don’t think we need the legislation. We have all the rules we need. We just need them enforced,” Bessent said on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures.

Bessent also said Nvidia needs a “dramatic shakeup”. Its board should go outside the company for its next chief executive, he said, as Reuters reported. He wants answers from the board and its outside counsel within 10 days. His question is whether Nvidia ignored warning signs of shell companies funnelling chips to China. Allies of Jensen Huang are meanwhile discussing his return.

Pressure on Lutnick grew on Sunday with a New York Times investigation by Ana Swanson, Aaron Krolik and Paul Mozur. Lutnick ran Cantor Fitzgerald for decades before handing it to his sons. The Times found that Cantor has worked with Southeast Asian data centre companies that serve Chinese clients.

One is Bitdeer, a Singaporean firm building a data centre called A201 in Malaysia’s Johor state. Cantor acted as a sales agent for Bitdeer’s equity offering of up to $1bn this year. A person with knowledge of the arrangement told the Times the site will likely serve Tencent. Renting chips this way is legal, and it sidesteps the ban on selling advanced chips directly to Chinese firms.

Lutnick is writing the rules that would decide whether that route stays open. Commerce has pushed for a narrower version than others in the administration wanted, people familiar with the talks told the Times. The Times found no evidence that Cantor’s investments influenced him. A Commerce spokeswoman said he acts in the best interests of the United States. He does not discuss department matters with his sons, she added.

On Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported how Huang built this route. It said the Southeast Asian data centres gave Chinese companies computing power and cover for alleged chip smuggling.

In January, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter told more than a dozen officials what Trump wanted on licence conditions for H200 exports to China, Semafor reported on Friday. People with access to an account of the call gave Semafor his words.

“I was with the president when he and Jensen discussed this so I want to let you know what the president wanted. He wants this to go fast,” Teter said, according to Semafor.

Nvidia called a rule that sellers know their cloud customers a “poison pill”, Semafor reported. It also pushed to raise the threshold for buyer checks to tens of thousands of chips. A Bureau of Industry and Security spokesperson told Semafor such talks with companies are “completely routine”. Nvidia declined to comment. Commerce had already halted its Megaspeed probe after Teter contacted a senior official, the Times reported earlier this month.

“It looks like he has been the barrier inside the government to stopping the flow of these Nvidia chips to China. And the question is why?” Representative Jim Himes said on CBS’s Face the Nation.

Republican John Moolenaar, who chairs the House China committee, said Lutnick and the whole Commerce Department need to answer questions. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, plan to ask why Lutnick declined to blacklist suspected smugglers, Representative Stephen Lynch told The Washington Post.

Senator Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, wrote to Lutnick on Sunday ahead of the Xi meeting, CNBC reported. She urged him to enforce export controls under the 2018 Export Control Reform Act and stop chips reaching barred companies.

“These failures to carry out the law help give away America’s technology advantage in AI,” Cantwell wrote.

Cantwell also pointed to Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2bn in Nvidia stock when Lutnick was nominated. She said the administration’s 25% fee on some Nvidia chip sales to China could create a financial incentive to approve exports. Commerce did not immediately respond to CNBC.

The Post also reported, citing a former administration official, that Bessent confronted Lutnick over why he had not acted despite instructions from Trump on three occasions. Bessent has said publicly that Commerce has the pen. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on 10 December.

The White House says it has complete confidence in Lutnick, according to Semafor. A senior US official told reporters the Nvidia scandal should have no bearing on the China trip.

#3203. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

#3202. Indonesian police reportedly found no Nvidia chips at Megaspeed’s unit

The Straits Times says the Megaspeed raid came at the FBI’s request, before Jensen Huang quit. Companies tied to Alice Huang have also bought into DeepSeek, The Information reported.

Indonesian police searched the local office of Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, The Straits Times reported on Monday. They found server racks but no Nvidia chips. The FBI had asked for the search earlier this year to trace chips Megaspeed bought.

The paper’s source is a senior Indonesian government official who asked not to be named. It calls the Megaspeed raid the first known enforcement action in Indonesia tied to the case. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Officers from the police’s criminal investigation department visited PT Megaspeed International Indonesia, the official said. Nobody seemed to have unpacked or used the racks.

The official alleged that Megaspeed entities shipped most of their Nvidia hardware to Indonesia. Investigators believe much of it then went on to China, possibly by private jet, he said. The head of the police’s international relations division declined to comment to the paper.

The raid came before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November. He had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed says she left in August 2025 and that it runs a lawful business.

Singapore’s digital minister, Josephine Teo, raised Megaspeed with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington last week. Both sides agreed to keep talking, the Straits Times reported.

Singapore has barred Alice Huang from returning, and its inquiry into Megaspeed and six other people goes on. Malaysia is investigating AI chips linked to the company. On 13 November it said it is working with Singapore and the US against chip smuggling.

Companies tied to Alice Huang also invested in DeepSeek, Claudia Chong reported for The Information on 13 November. The two firms are Century Litong and its Shanghai-listed parent, Jiangsu Lettall Electronics. The Information describes them as big suppliers of black-market Nvidia Blackwell chips in China.

DeepSeek staff introduced the two firms to its investors as critical to chip supply, according to the report. They joined DeepSeek’s 105.5bn yuan ($15.8bn) round through vehicles that investors such as Monolith Management set up. Lettall put in 95mn yuan this way. The full amount from the group is unclear.

Eduardo Baptista at Reuters reviewed more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, contracts and disclosures. He found projects worth over 23bn yuan ($3.2bn) built around restricted Nvidia H100, H200 and H800 chips. Reuters found no link between those projects and Megaspeed. Nvidia and China’s commerce ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says other departments wanted Megaspeed on the US trade blacklist for months, but Commerce had the pen. China denies the spying allegations. No authority has found that Megaspeed broke US rules.

Netflix has announced its slate of new movies and shows for the week ahead, and there's plenty to be excited about. From new originals, seasonal watches, and some library titles, you're spoilt for choice. So I'm picking the highlights.

This week my selections include one of the biggest movies of 2026, which blends horror and comedy, and displays the dangers of obsession. Or how about a new Netflix holiday original, adapted from a best-selling book, and pitched. The plot seems predictable, but it'll be good for some festive warmth.

Meanwhile, binge-watchers can sink their teeth into two newcomers at opposite ends of the spectrum. There's a new game show, which will speak to shopping addicts, and a limited series based on one of the decade's most infamous crypto scams (though in my books, anything crypto is a scam).

Finally, Netflix has a new fantasy animated flick that will be perfect for the whole family. It tells the timeless story of Cinderella from a whole new perspective. Proving that even a villainous figure can become a hero.

These are just some of the movies and shows heading to Netflix this week. Alongside my top picks, you’ll find a full schedule of everything new on Netflix over the next seven days. And for a complete overview, here’s a guide to everything new on Netflix in November 2026.

What it's about: Bear (Michael Johnston) is a timid music shop worker hopelessly infatuated with his colleague and friend, Nikki (Inde Navarrette). When he wishes on a junk shop trinket for Nikki to love him, his wish actually comes true, but his initial joy soon turns sour when getting the girl of his dreams comes with some seriously sinister consequences.

Why you should watch it: "Obsession" is one of the biggest movies of 2026. Produced on a sub-$1 million budget, it went on to gross more than $500 million worldwide, and Navarrette is firmly in the awards conversation. It marks director Curry Barker as a next-generation filmmaking talent to watch

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Watch "Obsession" on Netflix starting November 16

What it's about: No-nonsense Hannah Brookes (Leighton Meester) is hired as the bodyguard for action-movie star Jack Stapleton (Jared Padalecki) as the A-lister tries to avoid a relentless stalker over the holiday season. To keep Stapleton's family from worrying about his safety, the two pose as a couple, and predictably, the fake romance becomes a real love affair.

Why you should watch it: Netflix's new Christmas original is based on the novel "The Bodyguard" by Katherine Center and has a distinctive Hallmark vibe. Whether or not that's a selling point is a matter of personal preference, but the holiday flick looks like a charming, cozy watch for the winter season.

Watch "Guarding Stars" on Netflix starting November 18

What it's about: Netflix's latest glossy, overedited, competitive reality series is called "Win the Mall." Hosted by Haley Baylee, it sees 10 so-called "expert shoppers" battle for a huge cash prize in a shopping mall. Expect shopping-themed challenges and an urge for some retail therapy after watching. Special guests include Jonathan Van Ness, Salish Matter, and Lilly Singh

Why you should watch it: Netflix has been bolstering its competitive game show roster in recent years, and "Win the Mall" is the latest entry in the disposable stable. It doesn't look great, but it'll probably make for suitable background noise if you need a Netflix show to watch while doing chores.

Watch "Win the Mall" on Netflix starting November 18

What it's about: Based on the true story of financial fraud, "The Altruists" follows lovebirds Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner) and Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) as they create crypto exchange platform FTX, which collapsed in 2022 and was revealed to be a front for wire fraud, money laundering, and a litany of other white-collar crimes.

Why you should watch it: Netflix will hope "The Altruists" is met with a warmer reception than recent box office bomb "The Social Reckoning," which proved public interest in dramatic retellings of online wrongdoing isn't exactly high. Fortunately, this Netflix limited series appears to be hooked on the relationship between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, which might help it stand out. At least it'll be more evidence of what we all know: crypto bros suck.

Watch "The Altruists" on Netflix starting November 19

What it's about: A new twist on the "Cinderella" story, "Steps" reframes the fairy tale around Lilith, one of Cinder's stepsisters. When she accidentally transforms her other sister into a frog and throws the fantasy Kingdom into chaos, Lilith has to team up with Cinderella and a troll to save the day.

Why you should watch it: There's nothing novel about an animated movie putting a new spin on a classic story, but "Steps" looks like good family fun this Thanksgiving, and a solid streaming alternative to taking the whole family to see Disney's "Hexed" in theaters. It features a strong voice cast with Ali Wong, Amanda Seyfried, Daniel Radcliffe, Peter Dinklage and Bette Midler.

Watch "Steps" on Netflix starting November 20

"Mike Ward: Modest" (CA) (Netflix comedy special)

French-Canadian comic Mike Ward delivers an unapologetically honest set, from dating after divorce to living life to the fullest — one impulse at a time.

After moving to the countryside, Lucy hopes for a fresh start with her family — but a police visit and her husband's dark secret shatter her world.

A no-nonsense bodyguard heads to a Montana ranch with the famous actor she's protecting. But posing as a couple for Christmas soon sparks a real romance.

"The Law of Beasts" (PL) (Netflix series)

Panic returns to Poland as a convicted child murderer nears release, reigniting moral conflict between the case's lead investigator and its psychiatrist.

"Valentina and the 12 Signs" (BR) (Netflix series)

After a devastating breakup, Valentina decides to date one man from every zodiac sign. But the universe has other plans.

Part shopping spree, part social strategy, this high-gloss reality competition drops players into a living mall where they’ll fight to outshop, outsmart, and outlast one another — and only one will walk away with the keys to the ultimate prize.

The story of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, two hyper-smart, ambitious young idealists who tried to remake the global financial system in the blink of an eye - before they were accused of stealing $8 billion and became Gen Z's own Bonnie & Clyde.

"On Behalf of My Son" (BR) (Netflix film)

After her son crashes a bus, Vicentina sets out to find every victim's family, determined to apologize to them face-to-face while mourning her own loss.

"Primetime Preacher$" (Netflix documentary)

In the 1980s, televangelists Jim Bakker, Jerry Falwell, and Jimmy Swaggart transformed American religion and politics, until greed, rivalry, and scandal ignited a holy war that threatened their empires.

In this charmingly offbeat action comedy, Cinderella's "evil" stepsister Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother's wand and shatters the story as we know it.

#3199. Apple @ Work: The spiritual successor to the Xserve is here, thanks to Apple silicon and MLX

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

Open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being said, Siri is still far behind.

Look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post shows four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

That’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some new use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A company like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

The Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the company went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

In talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.

#3197. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3196. Plural raises €1bn for European start-ups in defence, energy and AI

The London firm’s third fund doubles its last one. Two-thirds goes into new early-stage bets and the rest into its breakout companies, from Helsing to Proxima Fusion.

Plural’s six partners: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty

Plural, the London-based venture firm run by former founders, has raised €1bn ($1.1bn). It will back European start-ups in energy, AI infrastructure, defence and health. It is the firm’s largest raise yet, almost four times its €260m first fund in 2022. Its second fund, in 2024, was €500m.

Plural announced the money on Monday on its website and in a press release. About two-thirds goes into its third early-stage fund. The rest goes into a new “opportunities” fund for its existing companies, partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih told TechCrunch.

“We’re convinced these frontier founders are capable of building Europe’s first trillion-dollar company, and we want to be backing them from day one,” Helioui said in the release.

Plural says each partner will lead a small number of new investments a year. Partner Sten Tamkivi told Tech.eu that Fund III should make 25 to 35 investments with six partners. Fund I made 31 with five.

The extra money goes deeper into each company, Tamkivi said. A software start-up can often prove its idea with a €1.5m seed round, he said. A fusion, hypersonics or chip company may need well over $20m to reach its first milestone.

Co-founder Taavet Hinrikus told Reuters the partners will look at AI infrastructure, including chip plants, plus robotics and defence.

“We do not pretend to know in which area the next great company will be built,” Hinrikus told Reuters.

Plural launched in June 2022, a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Its portfolio includes the defence company Helsing, which raised $1.8bn in July. Proxima Fusion closed a €411m round the same month. Plural also backs the chip start-up OLIX, The Exploration Company and the missile maker Hypersonica.

Its companies have raised more than €3bn in follow-on money in the past 12 months, Plural says. More than 100 European companies have raised rounds of $100m or more this year. About 10% of Plural’s portfolio is among them.

All six partners have built or run companies. Hinrikus co-founded Wise, Tamkivi co-founded Teleport and Ian Hogarth co-founded Songkick. Helioui ran Bigpoint, Namih co-founded HelixNano and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty is a former Uber executive. The firm has offices in London, Tallinn and Paris.

Backers of the second fund put in more than 125% of their earlier commitments, Helioui told Ingrid Lunden at Resilience Media. Endowments and foundations are the largest group of investors, at over 30% of the capital. Plural does not disclose its returns, Lunden reported.

The raise comes days after Sequoia closed its London office.

“It’s one firm’s decision about its office, not about where great companies get built,” Helioui told Resilience Media.

#3195. Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device

This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

On iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

The Lavazza Tabli is the "It" girl of 2026

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm Erin, and welcome to The Coffee Lab Episode 25, the series where we forget coffee snobbery. The Coffee Lab is all about making coffee fun. Join me as I help you kickstart your coffee journey!

Here at The Coffee Lab, I'm always eager to get my hands on the newest and most exciting coffee tech. So when I saw a commercial for the Lavazza Tabli on YouTube, I was instantly smitten. Yes. A commercial worked on me — I was influenced!

A few days later, I had the Lavazza Tabli in my hands, and everything was right in the world. At first, I needed to know how. How did the Lavazza Tabli work? If you're not sure what it does, let me give you a quick introduction: it's a pod machine... that doesn't use pods.

That's right. The Tabli uses 100% coffee "Tabs," shaped like hockey pucks, rather than plastic- or aluminum-encased ground coffee. This coffee is compacted so tightly that it keeps its shape. And don't wrinkle your nose — this coffee tastes genuinely incredible. I'm a hard-to-please coffee snob, and I've been singing the Tabli's praises since I tested it a few weeks ago. Here's why the Lavazza Tabli is one of my favorite coffee makers of 2026 — perhaps ever.

Of course, no one's claiming the Lavazza Tabli can make espresso better than a machine like the Lelit MaraX3, single-origin artisan beans, and a talented barista. That would be outrageous and untrue.

However, I am claiming that the Lavazza Tabli tastes a thousand times better than the best Keurig — I just tested the Keurig K-Mini Mate, and while it's tiny and easy, I would rather drink instant — and ten times better than the best Nespresso. Obviously, I don't have quantitative data to back that up, but can I interest you in a decibel counter for the volume of "Mmm" noises I made while drinking said coffees? Because the Tabli surely would win.

Unlike Nespresso and Keurig, Lavazza has just five "Tab" flavors: espresso intenso, qualita rossa, qualita oro, ristretto, and decaf. My favorite was oro. While Nespresso tastes so much better than Keurig, Nespresso shots are still a touch weak and stale, without the vivaciousness on the palate I look for in espresso.

This inexpensive machine uses compressed pucks of grounds to make some truly tasty coffee — without the wasteful pods.

The Tabli? Oh-so vivacious. So vivacious, in fact, that I would equate it to a party on my tongue. The shot is strong and full-bodied, like any Italian coffee tends to be, but with a delicate sweetness rounding out the mouthful. While the flavor depends on your "Tab", both the oro and the rossa were punchy yet delightfully drinkable.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I said this in my review, and I'll say it again, but I do wonder if, in time, Lavazza will introduce some kind of Tab-making machine: a press or compacter of some kind, so you can make your own "Tabs". That would be awesome. Catch me making coffee snobs choke on their espressos when I grind single-origin Yirgacheffe into Lavazza Tabs. Ha!

Like Nespresso and Keurig machines, the Lavazza Tabli requires zero cleanup. Well, unless you count removing a pod drawer and emptying it into your compost/trash as cleanup. I'm not sure I would.

Using the Tabli is as easy as this: pop a pod in, press go, drink coffee, empty drawer. Sure, you should probably clean the pod insert after every use, and you should definitely clean out the pod drawer every day (coffee gets moldy quickly), but in terms of scooping-out-wet-grounds-from-a-portafilter-basket-and-emptying-a-milky-drip-tray cleaning, it's minimal.

Although I adore everything about the Lavazza Tabli, there are still a few things I would recommend being aware of before biting the bullet.

One being the most obvious: the Tabli is only compatible with Lavazza-brand Tabs (for now). These are a dollar a pop, in line with Nespresso's original pods (around $0.90-$1) and cheaper than the Vertuo pods (up to $1.40 in some flavors). Keurig pods are around $0.50-$0.70 — but remember you can't recycle them for free, so you're out of pocket for caring about the planet. Great! Thanks, Keurig. Nothing says "There is no planet B" like forcing consumers to pay to recycle the plastic pods you make en masse.

Nespresso original and Keurig pods aren't patented, unlike Vertuo, so third parties can manufacture pods in a whole array of flavors.

The Lavazza Tabli machine itself is patented, which I presume extends to the Tabs themselves (boo! — but I get it). This means, if you buy the Tabli, you're locked into buying Lavazza's Tabs — just like a Nespresso Vertuo.

Right now, Lavazza only offers those five core flavors, so no specialty Tabs like fall favorite pumpkin spice or Christmas classics like eggnog or Irish cream. Of course, you can buy syrups to add to your drinks, but Nespresso makes flavored pods. This might be something worth knowing if you're a flavored coffee fanatic.

Would you try the Lavazza Tabli? Or do you love your Nespresso/Keurig machine too much to part with it?

I would personally buy the Lavazza Tabli. Oh yeah — I saved the best 'til last. It's just $129. No, not a typo. Yes, $129. This is almost incomprehensibly cheap... in the best way. The Nespresso CitiZ is $265, the Nespresso Pixie is $229, and the Keurig K-Supreme is $169.

#3193. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.
